Title: An Integrated Methodological Approach for Interpreting Used Oil Analysis in Diesel Engines
Snippet: Used oil analysis has established itself as a key tool in predictive maintenance for diesel engines [1], enabling the assessment of lubricant condition [2], the detection of wear indicators in internal components [3], and the monitoring of external contaminants [4]. 

Unlike traditional corrective and preventive maintenance approaches, where oil changes are scheduled at a fixed time or mileage intervals without considering the actual degradation of the lubricant, condition-based maintenance (CBM) has proven to be a more efficient strategy, allowing for the extension of oil service life [5,6], reduction in operating costs [7], and minimization of unexpected failures [8]. However, the practi-Lubricants 2025, 13, 169 2 of 17 cal interpretation of used oil analysis remains a challenge, primarily due to the lack of standardized methodologies for accurately evaluating lubricant degradation patterns [9]. 

Traditionally, studies have relied on predefined condemnation limits for key parameters, such as viscosity, Total Acid Number (TAN), Total Base Number (TBN), wear metal concentrations, and contaminants, such as water and silica [10][11][12][13]. However, these thresholds are often based on limited historical data and manufacturer recommendations, which do not always reflect the variability of real-world engine operating conditions, reducing diagnostic reliability. 

To overcome these limitations, advanced approaches based on statistical tools and artificial intelligence have been explored, including linear regression and correlation analysis [14][15][16], as well as Principal Component Analysis (PCA), which has proven effective in reducing data dimensionality and identifying lubricant degradation patterns [17][18][19]. Additionally, advances in machine learning have enabled the implementation of neural networks and predictive algorithms to anticipate diesel engine failures based on historical oil analysis data [20][21][22][23][24]. However, these approaches still have limitations, as most focus on identifying long-term degradation trends without addressing the detection of abrupt changes in lubricant conditions, which restricts their applicability in condition-based maintenance strategies.

Below is a synthesis of AI applications in lubrication that have achieved documented industrial-scale deployment or field rollouts, grouped by function and sector, with quantitative outcomes where available.

Summary overview
- Industrial-scale deployments in lubrication are most commonly found in predictive maintenance and condition monitoring for rotating equipment, digital-twin–enabled remaining useful life (RUL) management, and AIoT-enabled lubrication control and oil-change optimization, rather than pure lab demonstrations of novel lubricant chemistry. These deployments leverage oil analysis, sensor streams (vibration, temperature, pressure), SCADA, and machine learning models integrated into maintenance workflows across oil & gas, wind power, mining, hydraulics, and agricultural/industrial machinery. <cite id="889f9f69-0">Artificial intelligence-enabled digital twins in tribology combine physics-based models, real-time sensor data, and data-driven learning to enable near real-time prediction of lubrication regime transitions and remaining useful life with adaptive control and maintenance optimization</cite>.

Category 1: Oil condition monitoring and predictive maintenance with ML (enterprise/field scale)
- Oil & gas field deployment (Baker Hughes): <cite id="889f9f69-1">A digital twin–based predictive maintenance implementation on fracturing trucks by Baker Hughes used machine learning to distinguish between healthy and unhealthy pumps, yielding substantial cost savings and demonstrating practical benefits of AI-driven prognostics in a large-maintenance organization</cite>. While not exclusively lubricant-focused, the integration of ML on-site for asset health assessment and RUL informs lubrication and maintenance actions.
- Offshore wind farms: <cite id="6b617b73-2">A gearbox replacement case at the Teesside offshore wind farm (27 turbines) established a data management system integrating SCADA and condition-monitoring (CMS) data, built supervised learning models to predict similar failures, and reported lessons for failure detection and predictive modeling across the fleet</cite>. <cite id="6b617b73-3">Reviews of wind turbine accident/news datasets identify deep neural networks to predict lubricant pressure in gearboxes with higher accuracy than five alternative methods, enabling monitoring of log data and prediction of failures before they occur, and report applications of ML on real-world field data to predict defect occurrence, criticality, and type</cite>.
- Heavy industry and mining predictive maintenance: <cite id="889f9f69-1">Bibliometric and industry analyses emphasize AI-driven predictive maintenance in oil and gas, noting digital twin frameworks and ML for prognostic diagnostics and anomaly detection that enhance productivity, reduce downtime, and predict equipment life</cite>. <cite id="889f9f69-2">Recent AIoT work reports high-performance ANN/ANFIS models to predict lubricant life and system failures with correlation coefficient 0.99, opening opportunities for adoption of dynamic lubrication systems in mining and heavy industry</cite>. <cite id="889f9f69-2">Studies integrate IoT/AI for real-time predictive maintenance in mining environments and demonstrate that hybrid AIoT approaches support anomaly-conditioned classification in industrial diesel generators</cite>. <cite id="6b617b73-0">Machine learning classifiers (e.g., Naive Bayes 95.7% accuracy) on vibration data from a 750 kW wind turbine testbed show potential for gearbox fault diagnosis and highlight the need to validate approaches “in concert with diversity and in the real world,” bridging lab to field</cite>. <cite id="6b617b73-4">Practical applications of wind turbine gearbox condition monitoring include early detection to enable predictive maintenance, reducing downtime and costs in operations</cite>.

This is an explicit deployment pathway for lubrication maintenance decisions tied to sensor data and ML, applicable to oil and gas rotating equipment.
- Integration with used oil analysis and CBM: <cite id="d8042593-2">Advanced statistical/AI methods (PCA, neural networks) have been used on used oil analysis (TAN/TBN, metals, contaminants) to overcome limitations of fixed thresholds, enabling better condition-based maintenance that extends oil life, reduces costs, and minimizes unexpected failures compared to time- or mileage-based changes</cite>. <cite id="d8042593-4">In mining equipment predictive maintenance, ML-enhanced monitoring improved reliability indicators (higher MTBF, lower MTTR), and oil analysis trends (kinematic viscosity stability, metal content) supported adjustments to maintenance frequency (e.g., to every 200 h) and early detection of fretting wear</cite>. <cite id="d8042593-1">Despite ML advances in predictive maintenance, a gap remains in ML-specific oil analysis for underground mining diesel engines under real operating conditions—indicating active industry need and emerging deployment focus on this niche</cite>.

- Oil & gas and drilling fleets: <cite id="889f9f69-1">Enterprise implementations in oil and gas combine IIoT sensing, ML, and digital twins to predict RUL and guide maintenance strategies, with case evidence (e.g., fracturing trucks) demonstrating cost savings; literature synthesizes how ML and hybrid models are increasingly used for prognostics and anomaly detection</cite>.
- Offshore wind O&M: <cite id="6b617b73-2">Teesside case deployment integrated SCADA/CMS and ML for failure prediction and early detection at fleet scale</cite>. <cite id="6b617b73-3">Deep neural networks predicting lubricant pressure in gearboxes and supervised learning for failure prediction are documented in wind farm contexts, supporting proactive lubrication and maintenance</cite>.
- Mining and heavy-duty haulage: <cite id="889f9f69-2">AIoT and ML-based predictive maintenance reduce downtime and enable dynamic lubrication strategies; ANN/ANFIS models predict lubricant life and failures with high accuracy, opening opportunities for adoption in mining operations</cite>. <cite id="d8042593-4">ML-enhanced predictive maintenance correlates with improved MTBF/MTTR and informs lubricant maintenance intervals based on viscosity and metal content trends</cite>.

- Tribology digital twins for lubrication: <cite id="889f9f69-0">AI-enabled digital twins in tribology enable near real-time prediction of friction, wear, lubrication regime transitions, and RUL with adaptive control and optimized maintenance, addressing scalability and data-quality challenges that are central to enterprise rollouts</cite>.

What these deployments look like in practice (applications and outcomes)
- Oil condition monitoring with ML decision support: <cite id="d8042593-2">Neural networks and PCA on used oil parameters (TAN/TBN, metals, contaminants) improve detection of lubricant degradation and internal wear, enabling CBM that extends oil life, reduces costs, and lowers unexpected failures</cite>. <cite id="d8042593-4">In mining equipment, ML-driven projections and oil analysis trends support shifting maintenance frequency (e.g., to every 200 h), improving MTBF and reducing MTTR</cite>. <cite id="889f9f69-1">In oil and gas, ML/digital twin frameworks for predictive maintenance reduce downtime and enable strategic maintenance planning using real-time and historical data</cite>.
- Digital twin–driven RUL and lubrication triggers: <cite id="d8042593-0">A tribosystem digital twin using deep learning on sensor inputs (load, friction, temperature) predicts RUL with >95% test accuracy and is designed for in-field deployment to trigger automated maintenance, directly tying lubricant management to sensor-driven decisions</cite>.
- AIoT autolube and lubricant-life prediction: <cite id="889f9f69-2">ANN/ANFIS models predict lubricant life and failures with high correlation (0.99), enabling dynamic lubrication strategies in mining and heavy industry, with reports of improved system reliability and reduced downtime in manufacturing and mining</cite>. <cite id="889f9f69-2">Hybrid AIoT systems perform anomaly-conditioned classification and integrate monitoring with control for real-time predictive maintenance</cite>.
- Sector exemplars: <cite id="889f9f69-1">Baker Hughes’ ML-based pump health deployment in fracturing trucks yielded substantial cost savings, illustrating enterprise-scale adoption of predictive maintenance that affects lubrication scheduling</cite>. <cite id="6b617b73-2">At Teesside offshore wind, SCADA/CMS plus supervised ML built predictive models for gearbox failure, feeding O&M decisions and lubrication maintenance</cite>. <cite id="6b617b73-3">Wind farm studies include deep neural prediction of lubricant pressure in gearboxes and failure forecasting using real-world field data</cite>. <cite id="d8042593-3">Agricultural machinery telematics predicts optimal oil change intervals and wear with ML, indicating a clear path to field validation and deployment</cite>.

Limitations and maturity
- Data and integration hurdles: <cite id="889f9f69-0">Key challenges include data quality, computational burden, model interpretability, and scalability in AI-enabled digital twins for tribology, which must integrate physics, real-time sensing, and ML at system scale</cite>. <cite id="889f9f69-1">Industry analyses highlight the need for hybrid models and digital twins for prognostics and anomaly detection, with growing evidence of value but also emphasize the importance of data-driven, integrated architectures</cite>.
- Deployment gap areas: <cite id="d8042593-1">Despite broad ML advances, targeted ML models for used oil analysis to predict incipient failures in diesel engines of underground mining equipment remain underexplored, indicating a current gap between general predictive maintenance ML and lubricant-specific deployment in that sector</cite>. <cite id="6b617b73-0">Wind ML studies stress validation “in concert with diversity and in the real world,” underscoring that many promising models still move from lab testbeds to field deployment</cite>.
- Hybrid approaches and standards: <cite id="d8042593-2">AI methods (PCA, neural networks) complement traditional used oil thresholds by capturing degradation patterns across variable real-world conditions, supporting CBM and lubrication interval optimization</cite>.

Practical guidance for selecting and deploying AI in lubrication
- Start with high-signal data sources: <cite id="889f9f69-1">SCADA, CMS, and IIoT sensors for rotating equipment, combined with oil analysis labs (TAN/TBN, metals, particles, acidity), provide the strongest features for predictive maintenance and RUL models</cite>. <cite id="889f9f69-2">AIoT architectures that integrate sensing and analytics can deliver real-time predictive maintenance in mining and heavy industry</cite>.
- Favor deployment-ready patterns: <cite id="d8042593-0">Digital-twin RUL models trained on oil-test and sensor data can be embedded to trigger automated maintenance actions, directly affecting lubricant change intervals</cite>. <cite id="d8042593-2">ML-enhanced oil analysis reduces false triggers versus fixed thresholds and extends oil life while lowering unexpected failures</cite>.
- Validate at fleet scale: <cite id="6b617b73-2">Offshore wind deployments demonstrate supervised learning models built on farm-scale SCADA/CMS data to detect failures earlier and reduce downtime</cite>. <cite id="6b617b73-3">Wind studies using real-world data to predict defect occurrence, criticality, and type show how ML improves operational planning</cite>.
- Track outcomes with maintenance KPIs: <cite id="889f9f69-1">Enterprise rollouts in oil and gas report improved maintenance strategies via ML/digital twins, with cost savings and reduced downtime</cite>. <cite id="889f9f69-4">A manufacturing plant case showed 35% higher predictive accuracy, 40% unplanned downtime reduction, and 25% maintenance cost optimization from AI+DT</cite>. <cite id="d8042593-4">Mining implementations link ML to higher MTBF and lower MTTR, and adjust lubricant maintenance frequency based on oil data trends</cite>.

Takeaway
- Documented industrial-scale deployments exist across oil & gas, offshore wind, mining, and agricultural machinery, where ML-driven predictive maintenance, digital-twin RUL models, and AIoT lubrication systems are integrated into O&M workflows to optimize lubrication and reduce downtime. These applications move beyond lab demonstrations by running on real SCADA/CMS and oil-analysis data, triggering maintenance actions, and delivering quantifiable operational improvements. <cite id="889f9f69-1">Enterprise examples such as Baker Hughes’ ML-based predictive maintenance on fracturing trucks demonstrate cost savings and operational impact</cite>, and <cite id="6b617b73-2">fleet-scale wind deployments show supervised learning models operational on SCADA/CMS to forecast gearbox failures and expedite detection</cite>. <cite id="d8042593-0">Tribosystem digital twins with deep learning predict RUL from sensor/oil data with >95% accuracy and are designed for in-field deployment to trigger automated lubrication maintenance</cite>, while <cite id="889f9f69-2">autolube and lubricant-life prediction with ANN/ANFIS reach high accuracy and are being adopted in mining and heavy industry</cite>. Where gaps remain, they reflect sector-specific data and integration challenges rather than a lack of technical feasibility, and hybrid physics-informed, AI-enabled digital twin architectures are emerging as a robust pathway to scalable deployment. <cite id="889f9f69-0">AI-enabled digital twins in tribology address multi-physics, multi-scale lubrication challenges with real-time monitoring and adaptive decision-making, while acknowledging data quality, compute, and interpretability hurdles</cite>. </answer>

Title: A Review of Artificial Intelligence Enabled Digital-Twin Technologies in Tribology
Snippet: Artificial intelligence and digital twin technologies have emerged as transformative tools for engineering systems that require accurate prediction, real-time monitoring, and adaptive decision-making. In tribology, conventional wear mitigation approaches rely heavily on empirical testing, simplified analytical models, and periodic condition-based maintenance strategies. While these methods have supported decades of engineering practice, they struggle to capture the multi-scale, multi-physics nature of friction, wear, and lubrication under dynamically changing operating conditions. Limitations such as delayed fault detection, limited adaptability to unseen regimes, high experimental cost, and an inability to integrate real-time system feedback motivate the need for more intelligent and responsive frameworks. Recent advances in artificial intelligence-enabled digital twins address these challenges by combining physics-based models, real-time sensor data, and data-driven learning algorithms within a continuously updated virtual representation of the physical system. In tribological applications, such frameworks enable near real-time prediction of frictional behavior, wear evolution, lubrication regime transitions, and remaining useful life, while supporting adaptive control and optimized maintenance decisions. This review consolidates the current research literature on artificial intelligence-enabled digital twin applications in tribology and lubricated mechanical systems, with emphasis on sensing technologies, hybrid modeling approaches, data management strategies, and system architectures. Key challenges, including data quality, computational burden, model interpretability, and scalability, are discussed alongside emerging solutions. Through an in-depth synthesis of peer-reviewed studies, this paper highlights how the integration of artificial intelligence and digital twins offers a robust pathway toward more reliable, efficient, and sustainable tribological systems.

Title: Advancements in predictive maintenance in the oil and gas industry: A review of AI and data science applications
Snippet: The advent of AI-driven predictive maintenance systems has revolutionized the approach to equipment maintenance in the oil and gas industry. These systems leverage the power of Artificial Intelligence (AI), the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), and advanced analytics to predict equipment failures before they occur, thereby enhancing operational efficiency and reducing downtime. 

Jia, Wang, and Deng (2022) discuss the implementation of IIoT-based predictive maintenance in the oil and gas industry. 

Their study highlights the integration of machine learning and deep learning models to analyze vast amounts of historical and real-time data generated by equipment. This approach allows for accurate predictions of the Remaining Useful Life (RUL) of equipment, enabling timely maintenance actions. The predictive maintenance process they describe includes data acquisition, processing, training of machine learning models, equipment health assessment, RUL prediction, strategy formulation, and execution. Such a comprehensive process ensures that maintenance activities are data-driven and strategically planned. Keleko et al. (2022) provide a bibliometric analysis of AI and real-time predictive maintenance in Industry 4.0, emphasizing the growing importance of AI techniques in predictive maintenance. Their analysis reveals a significant trend towards the use of data-driven, hybrid models, and digital twin frameworks for prognostic diagnostics and anomaly detection. The study underscores the potential of AI in enhancing productivity, reducing machine downtime, and predicting equipment life, thereby contributing to cost savings and improved monitoring of production systems. 

Rao (2020) explores the use of a digital twin in predictive maintenance, illustrating how this technology can unlock significant value in the oil and gas sector. A digital twin is a virtual representation of a physical asset, which can be used for simulating, predicting, and optimizing the asset's performance. Rao's study showcases how engineers at Baker Hughes implemented predictive maintenance on fracturing trucks, using machine learning techniques to distinguish between healthy and unhealthy pumps, resulting in substantial cost savings. This example demonstrates the practical benefits of integrating digital twin technology with predictive maintenance. 

AI-driven predictive maintenance systems in the oil and gas industry are characterized by several key features. Firstly, they rely on the continuous monitoring of equipment conditions through sensors and IIoT, providing a wealth of data for analysis.

Title: Smart Autolube: Optimized machine learning-based pressure prediction for AIoT lubrication systems
Snippet: This approach has been shown to improve system reliability and reduce downtime in the context of predictive maintenance in manufacturing systems and heavy industrial machinery (Benhanifia et al., 2025;Henderson & Sanders, 2025). Recent research also highlights how the combination of IoT and AI in the form of Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) can improve the adaptability of systems, making them suitable for real-time predictive maintenance in mining environments (Muhammed et al., 2024;Ucar et al., 2024). Research by Kumar et al. (2025) shows that the combination of sensors with algorithms such as ANN and ANFIS is able to predict lubricant life and system failures with excellent performance (correlation coefficient 0.99), opening up opportunities for the adoption of dynamic lubrication systems in mining and heavy industry. As a form of integration of the two approaches, the concept of Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) has emerged as a framework that integrates data collection and analytical intelligence in a holistic manner (Awaisi et al., 2024). 

Some researchers have attempted to address lubrication challenges through predictive modeling. Singh et al. (2022) demonstrated the potential of machine learning in optimizing lubrication and wear, while Nguyen Thanh & Cho (2024) explored a hybrid AIoT approach for anomaly conditional classification in industrial diesel generators. Similarly, Surucu et al. (2023) applied deep learning in predictive maintenance to minimize machine downtime and potential losses, while Liu et al. (2024) proposed machine learning-based fault diagnosis for several components of a hydraulic system. These studies highlight the growing relevance of AIoT in lubrication monitoring, but most of the existing research is still limited to general predictive maintenance without a strong focus on autolube systems. 

A number of studies have explored the application of AI to the prediction of tribological parameters, including lubricant life and wear rate, but not many have explicitly targeted the prediction of lubrication pressure in autolube systems based on operational parameters such as temperature and voltage (Ardah et al., 2025;Rojas et al., 2025).

Title: Machine Learning-Enabled Digital Twin Framework for Predictive Intelligence in Smart Mechanical Systems
Snippet: This study investigates the integration of digital twin technology and machine learning for predictive analysis in smart mechanical systems. The research emphasizes the role of intelligent computational frameworks in improving industrial monitoring, predictive maintenance, and operational efficiency within Industry 4.0 environments. A qualitative content analysis approach was employed by reviewing scientific literature, industrial reports, and previous studies related to digital twins, artificial intelligence, and predictive analytics. The findings indicate that digital twin architectures supported by machine learning algorithms can significantly enhance real-time monitoring, fault prediction accuracy, and maintenance optimization. The integration of IoT devices, cloud computing, and intelligent analytics also improves industrial sustainability, reduces operational downtime, and supports data-driven decision-making processes. Furthermore, the study identifies several technological challenges, including cybersecurity risks, data integration complexity, and computational limitations. Overall, the proposed intelligent digital twin framework provides a promising approach for future industrial innovation and sustainable smart mechanical system management

Title: AI-Driven Predictive Maintenance for Smart Manufacturing Systems Using Digital Twin Technology
Snippet: The rapid advancements in Industry 4.0 and smart manufacturing systems have necessitated the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Digital Twin Technology (DTT) to enhance operational efficiency and predictive maintenance strategies. This study proposes an AI-driven predictive maintenance framework that leverages Digital Twin Technology to enable real-time monitoring, fault diagnosis, and failure prediction in industrial environments. The framework integrates machine learning (ML) models, deep learning techniques, and edge computing to analyze sensor data, detect anomalies, and optimize maintenance schedules. A reinforcement learning-based decision model is employed to dynamically adjust maintenance strategies, reducing downtime and extending equipment lifespan. Additionally, physics-informed AI models are incorporated into the digital twin architecture to simulate operational behaviours and predict potential failures with high accuracy. The proposed system is validated through a case study in a smart manufacturing plant, demonstrating a 35% improvement in predictive accuracy, 40% reduction in unplanned downtimes, and 25% optimization in maintenance costs compared to traditional predictive maintenance approaches. The findings indicate that the integration of AI and DTT significantly enhances the reliability and efficiency of cyber-physical manufacturing systems (CPMS), paving the way for more autonomous and intelligent industrial operations.

snippet.text: The rapid advancements in Industry 4.0 and smart manufacturing systems have necessitated the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Digital Twin Technology (DTT) to enhance operational efficiency and predictive maintenance strategies. This study proposes an AI-driven predictive maintenance framework that leverages Digital Twin Technology to enable real-time monitoring, fault diagnosis, and failure prediction in industrial environments. The framework integrates machine learning (ML) models, deep learning techniques, and edge computing to analyze sensor data, detect anomalies, and optimize maintenance schedules. A reinforcement learning-based decision model is employed to dynamically adjust maintenance strategies, reducing downtime and extending equipment lifespan. Additionally, physics-informed AI models are incorporated into the digital twin architecture to simulate operational behaviours and predict potential failures with high accuracy. The proposed system is validated through a case study in a smart manufacturing plant, demonstrating a 35% improvement in predictive accuracy, 40% reduction in unplanned downtimes, and 25% optimization in maintenance costs compared to traditional predictive maintenance approaches. The findings indicate that the integration of AI and DTT significantly enhances the reliability and efficiency of cyber-physical manufacturing systems (CPMS), paving the way for more autonomous and intelligent industrial operations.

documents.title: A Review of Artificial Intelligence Enabled Digital-Twin Technologies in Tribology
documents.snippet: Artificial intelligence and digital twin technologies have emerged as transformative tools for engineering systems that require accurate prediction, real-time monitoring, and adaptive decision-making. In tribology, conventional wear mitigation approaches rely heavily on empirical testing, simplified analytical models, and periodic condition-based maintenance strategies. While these methods have supported decades of engineering practice, they struggle to capture the multi-scale, multi-physics nature of friction, wear, and lubrication under dynamically changing operating conditions. Limitations such as delayed fault detection, limited adaptability to unseen regimes, high experimental cost, and an inability to integrate real-time system feedback motivate the need for more intelligent and responsive frameworks. Recent advances in artificial intelligence-enabled digital twins address these challenges by combining physics-based models, real-time sensor data, and data-driven learning algorithms within a continuously updated virtual representation of the physical system. In tribological applications, such frameworks enable near real-time prediction of frictional behavior, wear evolution, lubrication regime transitions, and remaining useful life, while supporting adaptive control and optimized maintenance decisions. This review consolidates the current research literature on artificial intelligence-enabled digital twin applications in tribology and lubricated mechanical systems, with emphasis on sensing technologies, hybrid modeling approaches, data management strategies, and system architectures. Key challenges, including data quality, computational burden, model interpretability, and scalability, are discussed alongside emerging solutions. Through an in-depth synthesis of peer-reviewed studies, this paper highlights how the integration of artificial intelligence and digital twins offers a robust pathway toward more reliable, efficient, and sustainable tribological systems.

documents.title: Advancements in predictive maintenance in the oil and gas industry: A review of AI and data science applications
documents.snippet:
The advent of AI-driven predictive maintenance systems has revolutionized the approach to equipment maintenance in the oil and gas industry. These systems leverage the power of Artificial Intelligence (AI), the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), and advanced analytics to predict equipment failures before they occur, thereby enhancing operational efficiency and reducing downtime. 

Jia, Wang, and Deng (2022) discuss the implementation of IIoT-based predictive maintenance in the oil and gas industry. 

Their study highlights the integration of machine learning and deep learning models to analyze vast amounts of historical and real-time data generated by equipment. This approach allows for accurate predictions of the Remaining Useful Life (RUL) of equipment, enabling timely maintenance actions. The predictive maintenance process they describe includes data acquisition, processing, training of machine learning models, equipment health assessment, RUL prediction, strategy formulation, and execution. Such a comprehensive process ensures that maintenance activities are data-driven and strategically planned. Keleko et al. (2022) provide a bibliometric analysis of AI and real-time predictive maintenance in Industry 4.0, emphasizing the growing importance of AI techniques in predictive maintenance. Their analysis reveals a significant trend towards the use of data-driven, hybrid models, and digital twin frameworks for prognostic diagnostics and anomaly detection. The study underscores the potential of AI in enhancing productivity, reducing machine downtime, and predicting equipment life, thereby contributing to cost savings and improved monitoring of production systems. 

Rao (2020) explores the use of a digital twin in predictive maintenance, illustrating how this technology can unlock significant value in the oil and gas sector. A digital twin is a virtual representation of a physical asset, which can be used for simulating, predicting, and optimizing the asset's performance. Rao's study showcases how engineers at Baker Hughes implemented predictive maintenance on fracturing trucks, using machine learning techniques to distinguish between healthy and unhealthy pumps, resulting in substantial cost savings. This example demonstrates the practical benefits of integrating digital twin technology with predictive maintenance. 

AI-driven predictive maintenance systems in the oil and gas industry are characterized by several key features. Firstly, they rely on the continuous monitoring of equipment conditions through sensors and IIoT, providing a wealth of data for analysis.

documents.title: Smart Autolube: Optimized machine learning-based pressure prediction for AIoT lubrication systems
documents.snippet:
This approach has been shown to improve system reliability and reduce downtime in the context of predictive maintenance in manufacturing systems and heavy industrial machinery (Benhanifia et al., 2025;Henderson & Sanders, 2025). Recent research also highlights how the combination of IoT and AI in the form of Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) can improve the adaptability of systems, making them suitable for real-time predictive maintenance in mining environments (Muhammed et al., 2024;Ucar et al., 2024). Research by Kumar et al. (2025) shows that the combination of sensors with algorithms such as ANN and ANFIS is able to predict lubricant life and system failures with excellent performance (correlation coefficient 0.99), opening up opportunities for the adoption of dynamic lubrication systems in mining and heavy industry. As a form of integration of the two approaches, the concept of Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) has emerged as a framework that integrates data collection and analytical intelligence in a holistic manner (Awaisi et al., 2024). 

Some researchers have attempted to address lubrication challenges through predictive modeling. Singh et al. (2022) demonstrated the potential of machine learning in optimizing lubrication and wear, while Nguyen Thanh & Cho (2024) explored a hybrid AIoT approach for anomaly conditional classification in industrial diesel generators. Similarly, Surucu et al. (2023) applied deep learning in predictive maintenance to minimize machine downtime and potential losses, while Liu et al. (2024) proposed machine learning-based fault diagnosis for several components of a hydraulic system. These studies highlight the growing relevance of AIoT in lubrication monitoring, but most of the existing research is still limited to general predictive maintenance without a strong focus on autolube systems. 

A number of studies have explored the application of AI to the prediction of tribological parameters, including lubricant life and wear rate, but not many have explicitly targeted the prediction of lubrication pressure in autolube systems based on operational parameters such as temperature and voltage (Ardah et al., 2025;Rojas et al., 2025).

documents.title: Machine Learning-Enabled Digital Twin Framework for Predictive Intelligence in Smart Mechanical Systems

The research emphasizes the role of intelligent computational frameworks in improving industrial monitoring, predictive maintenance, and operational efficiency within Industry 4.0 environments. A qualitative content analysis approach was employed by reviewing scientific literature, industrial reports, and previous studies related to digital twins, artificial intelligence, and predictive analytics. The findings indicate that digital twin architectures supported by machine learning algorithms can significantly enhance real-time monitoring, fault prediction accuracy, and maintenance optimization. The integration of IoT devices, cloud computing, and intelligent analytics also improves industrial sustainability, reduces operational downtime, and supports data-driven decision-making processes. Furthermore, the study identifies several technological challenges, including cybersecurity risks, data integration complexity, and computational limitations. Overall, the proposed intelligent digital twin framework provides a promising approach for future industrial innovation and sustainable smart mechanical system management

Title: Automated wind turbines gearbox condition monitoring: A comparative study of machine learning techniques based on vibration analysis
Snippet: Wind turbines play a role in the adoption of renewable energy production, but they are susceptible to shutdowns that require thorough monitoring. Gearbox failures are an issue leading to maintenance and operational downtime. This study investigates the application of machine learning methods to enhance the diagnosis of gearbox problems using vibration analysis. Through the application of fault scenarios that impact bearings and gears, the researchers successfully extracted time domain features from vibration data of a 750 kW turbine testbed in order to detect indications of damage. Support Vector Machine (SVM), Naive Bayes, and K Nearest Neighbour (KNN) machine learning models were used to classify gearbox faults. Among these models, Naive Bayes achieved an accuracy rate of 95.7%, which exceeded the established benchmarks. The probabilistic approach was able to successfully associate symptom characteristics with fault patterns. Intelligent monitoring systems could improve maintenance efficiency. This data-driven approach highlights the potential of machine learning in supporting wind power development by eliminating gearbox inefficiencies and improving turbine reliability, and further research is being conducted to ensure that this approach works in concert with diversity and in the real world. This shows how machine learning is contributing to advances in renewable energy by helping to analyze predictive problems and prevent costly gearbox failures.

Title: Mechanism analysis and optimisation strategy for the impact of gear oil cleanliness on the service life of wind turbine gearboxes
Snippet: The population targeted in this study consists of personnel involved in the operation and maintenance (O&M) of wind turbines, including maintenance technicians, engineers, supervisors, and maintenance managers. These individuals participate in gearbox inspection, oil sampling, lubrication handling, and maintenance scheduling. They were selected due to their practical, experience-based understanding of gear oil cleanliness and its influence on gearbox service life. The personnel included in the study represent different hierarchical levels within wind farm operations, enabling a comprehensive perspective from frontline technical practices to managerial decision-making.

Title: Data Insights from an Offshore Wind Turbine Gearbox Replacement
Snippet: Gearboxes are a complex, yet vital assembly for non-direct-drive offshore wind turbines, which are designed to last for the lifetime of the asset. However, recent studies indicate that they may have to be replaced as early as 6.5 years. Moreover, their contribution to offshore wind farm failures and downtime has been shown to be amongst the three most critical assemblies with the highest material cost required. An improved understanding of these premature failures and the ability to predict them in advance could reduce inspection and maintenance costs, as well as to help overcome many logistical and planning challenges. The objective of this paper is to present the lessons learnt from a gearbox exchange performed in one of the offshore wind turbines at Teesside offshore wind farm, comprising 27 2.3MW wind turbines. The paper takes a condition monitoring perspective and uses the identified spalling at the inner part of the planetary bearing as the governing failure mode. A data management system has been setup, incorporating all the operational data received, including maintenance log information and sensor data. A period of up to 2.5 years, prior to the the gearbox exchange, is examined for this study. SCADA and CMS data of the faulty turbine are compared against the wind farm, using statistical methods and machine learning techniques. Supervised learning models are built, which will help predict similar failures in the future. Results show how different data sources can contribute in gearbox failure diagnosis and help to expedite failure detection for Teesside offshore wind farm and similar wind turbine and gearbox types. This paper will be of interest to wind farm developers and operators to build predictive models from monitoring data that can forecast potential gearbox failures.

Title: Analyzing a Decade of Wind Turbine Accident News with Topic Modeling
Snippet: These studies applied data analytics, especially machine learning techniques, to improve the condition monitoring of wind turbines and to predict faults in different components. 

The work in [49] proposed a methodology to predict wind turbine defects at three different levels, including their occurrence, criticality, and type. The performance of different data mining methods was analyzed using real-world data from the field. 

The work in [50] developed a methodology based on deep neural networks to predict lubricant pressure in gearboxes, which provides higher prediction accuracy compared to five other methods. Supported by a control chart of prediction errors, the framework can monitor log data and predict gearbox failures before they occur. 

The work in [51] applied text mining to analyze wind turbine service history (operation and maintenance (O&M)) reports and identified failure-associated words and terms. The authors analyzed data from wind turbines with generator or gearbox issues and applied decision tree and random forest classifiers to identify contextual words in failure situations. The ultimate objective of this research was to automatically detect possible failures. The work in [51] is related to our research because of the use of text mining; while [51] focuses on O&M reports for a subset of possible types of accidents for operational planning, our research considers news accidents for all possible types of accidents for strategic planning. 

The work in [52] reviewed the literature on the application of machine learning (ML) in the monitoring of wind turbines. The authors reviewed and categorized the models into 144 research papers. The authors identified the most common data sources and model techniques and presented guidelines for selecting the most applicable ML techniques. 

The work in [53] proposed a diagnosis approach that uses deep learning to predict gearbox errors. Although deep learning models by definition require large training datasets, the system described in [53] is reported to achieve high prediction accuracy even with small data samples. 

The work in [54] utilized deep convolutional generative adversarial networks (DC-GANs) to supervise the quality of wind turbine generator bearings. Validated through a real wind turbine dataset, the method was designed to recognize atypical conditions in bearings. 

The work in [55] introduced a methodology to detect specific wind turbine defects using transfer learning algorithms. The advantages of the new transfer-learning method are presented.

Title: Automated wind turbines gearbox condition monitoring: A comparative study of machine learning techniques based on vibration analysis
Snippet: Wind turbines play a crucial role in the transition to renewable energy sources, aiding the global push for environmental sustainability [1,2]. Yet, their sustainable operations hinge greatly on their reliability and effectiveness. Among the hurdles that wind turbine operators face is identifying issues in the gearbox, as these can lead to repairs, downtime, and potentially disastrous breakdowns [3,4]. Wind turbines alleviate the environmental consequences of energy generation by transforming the kinetic energy of wind into electricity that is free from emissions [5,6]. Their rapid and significant growth has been propelled by advancements that have improved efficiency and economi-cs, establishing wind power as a crucial contributor to renewable energy [7][8][9]. Nevertheless, turbines are still vulnerable to numerous mechanical and electrical defects that pose a threat to their performance and reliability [10]. Environmental factors can cause damage to rotor blades, which can then reduce their aerodynamic efficiency [11,12]. Generators and bearings are susceptible to both electrical and mechanical deterioration [13]. 

The gearbox is a very fragile component that is prone to failure, which can lead to costly repairs, prolonged downtime, and even more damage [14]. Gearbox faults account for nearly 25% of wind turbine failures, with downtime costs estimated at $200,000 to $300,000 per incident [15]. These failures, often origi-nating from bearing defects or gear wear, can cause multimegawatt production losses and cripple wind farm productivity [16]. Gearboxes are especially rotate to failure compared to other components in the drivetrain due to their complex design and substantial load-bearing capacity. Researchers have conducted a significant amount of research to develop advanced methods for identifying problems in gearboxes, aiming to enhance the dependability of turbines [17,18]. Advancements in signal processing and machine learning hold immense promise for timely anomaly detection and proactive maintenance [19,20]. 

Wind turbine gearbox condition monitoring is critical in maintaining the reliability and efficiency of wind power systems. Practical applications of this research are within several essential areas of the industry. With early detection of issues before they become severe failures, predictive maintenance strategies can be facilitated to reduce downtime and related maintenance costs directly.

Their rapid and significant growth has been propelled by advancements that have improved efficiency and economi-cs, establishing wind power as a crucial contributor to renewable energy [7][8][9]. Practical applications of this research are within several essential areas of the industry. Title: Lifetime Prediction Using a Tribology-Aware, Deep Learning-Based Digital Twin of Ball Bearing-Like Tribosystems in Oil and Gas
Snippet: The recent decline in crude oil prices due to global competition and COVID-19-related demand issues has highlighted the need for the efficient operation of an oil and gas plant. One such avenue is accurate predictions about the remaining useful life (RUL) of components used in oil and gas plants. A tribosystem is comprised of the surfaces in relative motion and the lubricant between them. Lubricant oils play a significant role in keeping any tribosystem such as bearings and gears working smoothly over the lifetime of the oil and gas plant. The lubricant oil needs replenishment from time to time to avoid component breakdown due to the increased presence of wear debris and friction between the sliding surfaces of bearings and gears. Traditionally, this oil change is carried out at pre-determined times. This paper explored the possibilities of employing machine learning to predict early failure behavior in sensor-instrumented tribosystems. Specifically, deep learning and tribological data obtained from sensors deployed on the components can provide more accurate predictions about the RUL of the tribosystem. This automated maintenance can improve the overall efficiency of the component. The present study aimed to develop a deep learning-based digital twin for accurately predicting the RUL of a tribosystem comprised of a ball bearing-like test apparatus, a four-ball tester, and lubricant oil. A commercial lubricant used in the offshore oil and gas components was tested for its extreme pressure performance, and its welding load was measured using a four-ball tester. Three accelerated deterioration tests was carried out on the four-ball tester at a load below the welding load. Based on the wear scar measurements obtained from the experimental tests, the RUL data were used to train a multivariate convolutional neural network (CNN). The training accuracy of the model was above 99%, and the testing accuracy was above 95%. This work involved the model-free learning prediction of the remaining useful lifetime of ball bearing-type contacts as a function of key sensor input data (i.e., load, friction, temperature). This model can be deployed for in-field tribological machine elements to trigger automated maintenance without explicitly measuring the wear phenomenon.

Title: Machine Learning-Based Oil Analysis for Underground Mining Equipment
Snippet: All these factors affect both data quality and sensing strategy. Even when specific maintenance optimization models for heavy-duty diesel engines have been developed, they have been based on stochastic processes rather than machine learning techniques [32]. 

Identified research gap: Although there are studies applying machine learning to vibration, electrical current, and operational variables analysis for predictive maintenance of engines in various industrial sectors [8,[10][11][12], as well as research addressing oil analysis as a condition monitoring technique in mining equipment from statistical and threshold-based approaches [33], no work developing machine learning models specifically oriented toward oil analysis for failure prediction in diesel engines of underground mining equipment is identified in the reviewed literature. The combination of oil analysis (wear parameters, contamination, and lubricant degradation) with advanced machine learning techniques remains unexplored in this particular operational context. This occurs despite oil analysis being one of the most accessible and widely used monitoring techniques in the mining sector due to its ability to detect internal wear without the need for invasive instrumentation, and despite sensor data being already used in other sectors to automatically identify anomalous operating conditions with high precision [34][35][36]. 

Consequently, a research opportunity exists to develop machine learning approaches that, based on historical oil analysis data and associated operational variables, can predict incipient failures in diesel engines of underground mining equipment. In this way, the gap between the predictive capabilities of artificial intelligence and the practical maintenance needs of this sector would be closed. This gap defines the research space that the present work seeks to cover. 

In summary, the literature demonstrates four relevant findings. First, artificial intelligence has substantially improved the capacity to detect and forecast failures in complex industrial assets. Second, engines and rotating systems can be effectively monitored using current, vibration, and operational variables, especially with deep or ensemble models. Third, the most recent trend points toward integrating prediction with operational decisionmaking through inventories, digital twins, and prescriptive maintenance. Fourth, despite these advances, a lack of studies specifically focused on the use of machine learning applied to oil analysis for diesel engines in underground mining equipment under real operating conditions persists. This gap defines the research space that this work seeks to address.

Title: An Integrated Methodological Approach for Interpreting Used Oil Analysis in Diesel Engines
Snippet: Used oil analysis has established itself as a key tool in predictive maintenance for diesel engines [1], enabling the assessment of lubricant condition [2], the detection of wear indicators in internal components [3], and the monitoring of external contaminants [4]. 

Unlike traditional corrective and preventive maintenance approaches, where oil changes are scheduled at a fixed time or mileage intervals without considering the actual degradation of the lubricant, condition-based maintenance (CBM) has proven to be a more efficient strategy, allowing for the extension of oil service life [5,6], reduction in operating costs [7], and minimization of unexpected failures [8]. However, the practi-Lubricants 2025, 13, 169 2 of 17 cal interpretation of used oil analysis remains a challenge, primarily due to the lack of standardized methodologies for accurately evaluating lubricant degradation patterns [9]. 

Traditionally, studies have relied on predefined condemnation limits for key parameters, such as viscosity, Total Acid Number (TAN), Total Base Number (TBN), wear metal concentrations, and contaminants, such as water and silica [10][11][12][13]. However, these thresholds are often based on limited historical data and manufacturer recommendations, which do not always reflect the variability of real-world engine operating conditions, reducing diagnostic reliability. 

To overcome these limitations, advanced approaches based on statistical tools and artificial intelligence have been explored, including linear regression and correlation analysis [14][15][16], as well as Principal Component Analysis (PCA), which has proven effective in reducing data dimensionality and identifying lubricant degradation patterns [17][18][19]. Additionally, advances in machine learning have enabled the implementation of neural networks and predictive algorithms to anticipate diesel engine failures based on historical oil analysis data [20][21][22][23][24]. However, these approaches still have limitations, as most focus on identifying long-term degradation trends without addressing the detection of abrupt changes in lubricant conditions, which restricts their applicability in condition-based maintenance strategies.

Title: Technology for extending the life cycle of agricultural machinery based on software training
Snippet: Introduction. The average age of machinery in the agro-industrial and mining complexes often exceeds its service life, which requires maintaining operability and improving technical and economic indicators. Up to 40% of equipment failures are related to the power plant and drive system, where oil plays a key role. Purpose of the research. This study is aimed at solving the most important problem of maintenance of agricultural and industrial machinery in conditions of increased load and aging of equipment. The main focus is on monitoring the lubrication systems of internal combustion engines and transmissions, which account for up to 40% of equipment failures. To improve operational efficiency and reduce wear, it is proposed to develop a telematics system for evaluating the properties of lubricants in real time. Materials and Methods. The research combines the approaches of tribology and data science. Existing real-time oil monitoring methods such as SOAP and JOAP were analyzed and limitations such as cost and data volume were identified. A new hardware and software solution has been developed, including sensors for measuring the acidity of oil and the concentration of solid particles. Using machine learning algorithms, the system predicts optimal oil change intervals and evaluates wear without the need for disassembly. Results. Preliminary results show that the system effectively monitors key properties of the lubricant, including acidity and particle size. Real-time data processing revealed patterns of deterioration in oil quality associated with the degree of wear, which allows timely maintenance. The predictive model, developed on the basis of historical data, provides high accuracy in predicting lubricant characteristics and wear thresholds. Initial modeling suggests that the service life of the equipment may increase by 15–20%, and downtime may be reduced by up to 30%. Conclusions. The developed system offers a comprehensive solution for quality management of lubricants and prevention of critical equipment failures. Thanks to real-time monitoring and machine learning, this approach provides increased reliability and reduces maintenance costs. Future work includes field tests of agricultural and industrial equipment to confirm these findings.

Title: Predictive Maintenance in Underground Mining Equipment Using Artificial Intelligence
Snippet: Figure 3 illustrates the direct relationship between operational reliability indicators and maintenance effectiveness. An increase in Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) reflects higher equipment reliability, while a decrease in Mean Time To Repair (MTTR) suggests improvements in maintainability. These results underscore the need to integrate artificial intelligence models capable of accurately predicting failure events, enabling more efficient maintenance planning and data-driven technical decision-making. This strategy would contribute to increased equipment availability and, consequently, to optimized performance in demanding operational contexts such as underground mining. 

Figure 6 displays the failure projection obtained using an optimized ARIMA model. The training data (blue line) exhibit high variability, whereas the actual observations (green line) reflect a more stable trend. The generated predictions (red line) for May 2024 exhibit a generally stable trend with minor fluctuations, indicating a low and stable probability of failure for the analyzed components. These results reinforce the appropriateness of maintaining the current predictive maintenance strategy, complemented by continuous monitoring to enable timely interventions and minimize the risk of critical failures. Figure 8 analyzes the evolution of kinematic viscosity at 100 • C as a function of oil service hours, using data processed through machine learning techniques. Two operational periods were compared: one before preventive maintenance adjustment and another after. The results show that in both cases, viscosity remains within the established technical limits (10.4 to 20.2 cSt), though with greater dispersion in the earlier period. This pattern suggests improved thermal stability of the lubricant in the current period and it supports adjusting the maintenance frequency to once every 200 h. Figure 9 shows the time-based evolution of six metals in the lubricating oil (Al, Cu, Cr, Sn, Pb, and Fe), correlated with equipment operating hours. In most cases, concentrations remain within the manufacturer-defined operational ranges. However, a moderate increase in iron (Fe) and chromium (Cr) levels is observed, along with a slight upward trend in aluminum (Al) and copper (Cu) during specific phases of the operating cycle. This may be associated with fretting wear on internal components such as bearings, heat-treated surfaces, and aluminum alloy components. These results highlight the utility of oil analysis as an early indicator of mechanical degradation.

Below is a synthesis of documented operational performance advantages of AI applications in lubrication over traditional non-AI methods, with evidence from field studies, lab frameworks, and system integrations. Where possible, we report quantitative deltas (reduction/increase percentages, time savings, error reductions) and link them to concrete operational outcomes (downtime, maintenance cost, availability, reliability, and safety).

1) AI-enhanced lubricant condition monitoring and oil analysis
- Speed and accuracy gains over conventional lab workflows: An integrated system that couples traditional oil diagnostics (optical emission spectroscopy, particle counting, viscosity/density, FT‑IR) with an AI model for gearbox condition monitoring demonstrated that AI support “can effectively support diagnoses, reduce processing time by 60%, and minimize human errors,” while improving knowledge sharing and reporting consistency compared to traditional expert-only evaluations <cite id="613fefb0-0">An integrated system combining oil diagnostics with an AI model reduced processing time by 60% and minimized human errors while improving consistency and clarity in reporting</cite>. 
- Beyond manual thresholds, AI/ML brings predictive power to oil analysis: Studies in diesel engine lubricants show that screening spectroscopic features via correlation analysis, information entropy, and lubricant degradation analysis before feeding an SVM improves both accuracy and efficiency of remaining useful life (RUL) prediction versus raw, uncurated datasets, indicating that AI-driven feature engineering and modeling outperform conventional “rule-of-thumb” thresholds in precision and throughput <cite id="613fefb0-1">An SVM-based RUL model for lubricating oil, built after screening atomic emission spectroscopy data using correlation analysis, information entropy, and degradation analysis, showed significantly improved accuracy and efficiency versus raw data</cite> <cite id="613fefb0-2">A parameter selection method using information entropy, correlation analysis, and lubricant deterioration analysis, combined with an SVM, improved RUL prediction accuracy and efficiency</cite>. 
- Practical interpretation and CBM benefits: Used oil analysis is already a mature technology for wear detection and lubricant health, but traditional diagnostic limits arise because fixed thresholds (e.g., viscosity, TAN/TBN, wear metals, water/silica) may not reflect real-world operating variability. Incorporating statistical tools and AI (e.g., PCA, neural networks) improves degradation pattern identification and failure anticipation; the literature specifically notes that AI-supported approaches address diagnostic reliability gaps and enable condition-based maintenance to extend oil life, reduce operating costs, and minimize unexpected failures compared to fixed-interval maintenance <cite id="613fefb0-3">Traditional oil analysis thresholds based on limited historical data reduce diagnostic reliability in varied operating conditions; statistical/AI methods (PCA, neural networks) enhance degradation pattern identification, enabling CBM to extend oil service life, reduce operating costs, and minimize unexpected failures</cite> <cite id="613fefb0-4">Oil analysis (spectroscopy, ferrography, viscosity, etc.) is widely used for condition monitoring; recent investigations target automated fault detection to augment mature techniques</cite>.

2) AIoT-enabled smart autolube and adaptive lubrication control
- Reliability, downtime, and maintenance optimization: AIoT-based smart autolube that integrates pressure/temperature/voltage sensors with machine learning (Random Forest/Gradient Boosting) for real-time lubrication pressure prediction achieved high accuracy (R² up to 0.9816) and enabled condition-adaptive lubrication decisions. The documented operational implications include optimizing maintenance schedules and improving machine life in heavy industry, with clear benefits for environments like mining where lubrication failures cause large losses; the system explicitly targets the reduction of downtime and associated costs through predictive, rather than time-based, lubrication strategies <cite id="3f1288dc-2">An AIoT smart autolube system with ML models achieved real-time lubrication pressure prediction accuracy (R² to 0.9816) and enabled condition-adaptive lubrication decisions with SHAP-explainable feature contributions</cite> <cite id="3f1288dc-1">Combining sensors with ANN/ANFIS predicted lubricant life and system failures with high correlation (0.99), supporting dynamic lubrication systems to reduce downtime in mining and heavy industry</cite> <cite id="3f1288dc-3">By replacing time-based with predictive condition-based lubrication, the AIoT smart autolube addresses limitations of conventional PLC-based autolube (cost/complexity) and supports reliability and cost efficiency</cite> <cite id="3f1288dc-4">The modular AIoT architecture enables offline/online operation and intelligent, adaptive correction of lubrication needs, improving practical viability for industrial implementation</cite>. 
- Benchmarking vs. traditional autolube: The same work emphasizes that commercial PLC autolubes are “often expensive, complex, and do not meet the needs of mining customers,” motivating a flexible, economical AIoT approach whose core advantage is adaptive, data-driven control of lubrication delivery aligned to actual operating conditions—enabling earlier intervention before pressure/condition degradation that would otherwise cause unplanned downtime <cite id="3f1288dc-3">Commercial PLC autolubes are costly and complex for mining; the AIoT approach provides a flexible, economical, context-aware alternative enabling adaptive lubrication control</cite>.

3) Predictive maintenance in gears and rotating equipment: quantified operational benefits transferable to lubrication
- Gearbox downtime and cost impact: Gearbox failures constitute a large share of wind turbine downtime and repair costs; AI-enabled predictive maintenance frameworks using vibration/SCADA data have delivered measurable operational improvements, including earlier fault warnings and reduced unscheduled maintenance, which by extension improve lubrication management because gearbox health is tightly coupled to lubricant condition and oil change strategies <cite id="00e678c6-0">Gearbox maintenance is a high priority due to ~20% of total downtime in wind turbines, with reactive maintenance costs 15–20% of turbine price; predictive strategies are essential to avoid weeks-long downtime and revenue loss</cite> <cite id="00e678c6-4">In a real wind farm, ANN models trained on SCADA data identified gearbox faults before breakdowns and reduced unscheduled maintenance by 30% with accurate predictions; decision-tree models achieved 95% accuracy, reducing downtime and repair costs</cite>. 
- Early warning windows and availability uplift: AI-driven gearbox health models have achieved early fault warnings up to 18 h 33 min before failures, enabling lubricant and maintenance interventions that avoid breakdowns; such predictive capabilities reduce maintenance frequency when risks are low and increase intervention precision where lubricant degradation or wear is detected, improving equipment availability compared to routine, calendar-based maintenance <cite id="00e678c6-3">An intelligent O&M framework with WOA‑TCN‑Attention predicted gearbox faults with early warnings up to 18 h 33 min and high accuracy, validating practical applicability in a wind farm</cite>. 
- Mining case with direct AI/ML PdM outcomes: In underground mining, an AI predictive maintenance framework integrating IoT sensors (including oil analysis and wear parameters) with machine learning reduced maintenance costs by 8% and increased equipment availability by 10% using empirical, real-operations data, directly evidencing operational advantages over traditional reactive or fixed-interval approaches; since lubrication is a primary factor in rotating equipment reliability, these savings are closely tied to improved lubrication monitoring and adaptive lubrication strategies <cite id="6810e879-1">An AI predictive maintenance framework in underground mining reduced maintenance costs by 8% and increased equipment availability by 10% using IoT sensors (temperature, pressure, oil analysis, wear) and machine learning, cutting unplanned downtime</cite>.

4) Mechanisms enabling AI’s operational edge
- Data-driven failure anticipation and RUL: AI models leverage multi-sensor and oil analysis data (spectroscopy, wear particles, viscosity, contamination) to detect incipient degradation and predict RUL, allowing lubrication intervals and oil formulations to be tailored to actual condition rather than fixed schedules; this yields fewer oil changes, lower lubricant consumption, and lower risk of failure compared to traditional threshold-based policies <cite id="613fefb0-0">AI integrated with statistical oil diagnostics overcomes long analysis times and subjective interpretation, reducing processing time by 60% and human error while improving diagnostic consistency</cite> <cite id="613fefb0-3">AI/statistical methods (e.g., PCA, neural networks) improve degradation pattern identification and enable CBM to extend oil service life, reduce operating costs, and minimize unexpected failures versus fixed-interval maintenance</cite> <cite id="613fefb0-1">Curated spectroscopy features with SVM improved lubricant RUL prediction accuracy and efficiency</cite>. 
- Explainable, actionable control: SHAP and feature attribution in AIoT autolube systems clarify how pressure, lag features, and rolling statistics drive predictions, enabling operators to adjust lubrication dosing and interval thresholds based on actual operating state rather than one-size policies; such closed-loop, explainable control improves reliability and reduces surprise downtime from starvation or excess lubrication <cite id="3f1288dc-2">SHAP analysis showed pressure lag and rolling statistics significantly and positively affect lubrication pressure predictions, supporting reliable, condition-adaptive lubrication decisions</cite>. 
- Industrial adoption evidence: Field trials and SCADA-based deployments in wind farms and mining demonstrate that AI predictive models can be integrated into existing operations with measurable savings in maintenance cost and downtime, and in some cases large early-warning windows for component failure—capabilities that translate directly to better lubrication management and planning <cite id="00e678c6-4">Deployed ANN models reduced unscheduled maintenance by 30% and accurately predicted gearbox faults in a wind farm</cite> <cite id="6810e879-1">AI PdM in underground mining reduced maintenance costs by 8% and increased equipment availability by 10%, with empirical data from actual operations</cite>. 

5) Limitations and context
- Data and deployment constraints: AIoT smart autolube benefits are contingent on quality sensor data, sufficient samples, and integration flexibility; small datasets (e.g., 720 samples) and limited parameter coverage can constrain generalization, and explainability is important for operator trust and safe deployment in safety-critical environments <cite id="3f1288dc-2">The study used 720 samples with Random Forest and Gradient Boosting, showing R² to 0.9816; limitations include dataset size and need for broader sensor integration, with SHAP providing interpretability</cite> <cite id="3f1288dc-3">Commercial PLC autolubes are costly/complex; the AIoT approach targets flexibility and cost efficiency while predicting lubrication pressure accurately</cite>. 
- Maturity by domain: Oil analysis remains a mature technology; AI complements it by handling variability and providing predictive insights, rather than replacing validated lab methods outright. Sectoral reviews emphasize that while AI-driven predictive maintenance is transformative, data quality, cost-effectiveness, and scalability are ongoing challenges—especially in sparse-data or harsh environments like underground mining—so realized savings depend on robust data pipelines and domain integration <cite id="613fefb0-3">Used oil analysis is mature; AI/statistical methods address diagnostic reliability and enable CBM to reduce cost and downtime</cite> <cite id="6810e879-2">AI-based PdM in mining shows high accuracies and cost/efficiency gains but faces data quality, cost, and scalability challenges; adaptable models and real-time decision-making are needed</cite>.

Summary of documented operational advantages where AI outperforms traditional non-AI lubrication methods
- Faster and more reliable lubricant diagnostics than manual/threshold-only methods, reducing analysis time by up to 60% and human error, and improving consistency and decision repeatability in oil diagnostics for gearboxes and engines <cite id="613fefb0-0">An integrated AI with oil diagnostics reduced processing time by 60% and minimized human errors while improving diagnostic consistency</cite>.

Practical implications
- For lubrication leaders, the strongest documented advantages of AI are reduced diagnostic cycle time and error, extended oil life via accurate RUL and contamination/wear detection, and lower downtime and maintenance costs through early-warning and condition-adaptive lubrication and maintenance scheduling in rotating equipment. Title: An Integrated Methodological Approach for Interpreting Used Oil Analysis in Diesel Engines
Snippet: Used oil analysis has established itself as a key tool in predictive maintenance for diesel engines [1], enabling the assessment of lubricant condition [2], the detection of wear indicators in internal components [3], and the monitoring of external contaminants [4]. 

Unlike traditional corrective and preventive maintenance approaches, where oil changes are scheduled at a fixed time or mileage intervals without considering the actual degradation of the lubricant, condition-based maintenance (CBM) has proven to be a more efficient strategy, allowing for the extension of oil service life [5,6], reduction in operating costs [7], and minimization of unexpected failures [8]. However, the practi-Lubricants 2025, 13, 169 2 of 17 cal interpretation of used oil analysis remains a challenge, primarily due to the lack of standardized methodologies for accurately evaluating lubricant degradation patterns [9]. 

Traditionally, studies have relied on predefined condemnation limits for key parameters, such as viscosity, Total Acid Number (TAN), Total Base Number (TBN), wear metal concentrations, and contaminants, such as water and silica [10][11][12][13]. However, these thresholds are often based on limited historical data and manufacturer recommendations, which do not always reflect the variability of real-world engine operating conditions, reducing diagnostic reliability. 

To overcome these limitations, advanced approaches based on statistical tools and artificial intelligence have been explored, including linear regression and correlation analysis [14][15][16], as well as Principal Component Analysis (PCA), which has proven effective in reducing data dimensionality and identifying lubricant degradation patterns [17][18][19]. Additionally, advances in machine learning have enabled the implementation of neural networks and predictive algorithms to anticipate diesel engine failures based on historical oil analysis data [20][21][22][23][24]. However, these approaches still have limitations, as most focus on identifying long-term degradation trends without addressing the detection of abrupt changes in lubricant conditions, which restricts their applicability in condition-based maintenance strategies.
</snippet>

Title: Smart Autolube: Optimized machine learning-based pressure prediction for AIoT lubrication systems
Snippet: This research successfully develops and implements an AIoT-based smart autolube system that integrates pressure, temperature, and voltage sensors with advanced machine learning models, namely RFR and GBR. Through the approaches of feature engineering, extreme fine tuning, and explainable artificial intelligence, the system is not only able to predict lubrication pressure in real time with high accuracy (R² to 0.9816) but also provides a transparent interpretation of the contribution of features to the prediction results using the SHAP method. The results of the experiment show that the trend features, the pressure lag (lag_1 and lag_2) and the rolling statistics (mean and standard deviation) contribute significantly to the improvement of the model performance. The SHAP value also shows that these features consistently positively affect the prediction results, supporting the reliability of condition-adaptive lubrication system decisions. 

The practical implications of this study are particularly relevant in the context of heavy industry, especially mining, where downtime due to lubrication failures can result in large losses. By integrating this system, operators can optimize maintenance schedules and improve machine life. However, the study has several limitations, including the limited number of datasets (720 samples), the flexibility of AIoT integration and hyperparameter tuning can increase the computational load, and focusing only on pressure parameters as the prediction target may ignore other variables such as lubricant flow, mechanical condition of the pump, or vibration. These limitations indicate the need for larger, more diverse data sets and broader sensor integration

Commercial solutions based on programmable logic controllers (PLCs) are available, but they are often expensive, complex, and do not meet the needs of mining customers, who are sensitive to cost, time efficiency, and limited technical resources (Sinitò et al., 2023). Therefore, a new approach that is more flexible, economical, and contextualized is needed. 

To address this gap, this study developed an AIoT-based Smart Autolube that integrates pressure, temperature, and voltage sensors into a single real-time monitoring system and applies machine learning algorithms to predict lubrication pressure in an accurate and adaptive manner. The two models used and compared were the Random Forest Regressor and the Gradient Boosting Regressor. Random Forest is known for its ability to robustly handle multivariable data and is tolerant of overfitting (Wu et al., 2025), while Gradient Boosting excels at identifying highly accurate nonlinear patterns in energy and industrial forecasting systems (Krishnan et al., 2024;Val et al., 2024). By comparing the two models in the real-world context of an autolube system, this study aims to provide lubrication that is not only automatic, but also adaptive, efficient, and intelligent, thus driving the transformation from a time-based lubrication system to a predictive condition-based lubrication system that is practical and applicable in a modern mining and manufacturing environment that demands high reliability and cost efficiency.
