Snippet: Wind turbines play a crucial role in the transition to renewable energy sources, aiding the global push for environmental sustainability [1,2]. Yet, their sustainable operations hinge greatly on their reliability and effectiveness. Among the hurdles that wind turbine operators face is identifying issues in the gearbox, as these can lead to repairs, downtime, and potentially disastrous breakdowns [3,4]. Wind turbines alleviate the environmental consequences of energy generation by transforming the kinetic energy of wind into electricity that is free from emissions [5,6]. Their rapid and significant growth has been propelled by advancements that have improved efficiency and economi-cs, establishing wind power as a crucial contributor to renewable energy [7][8][9]. Nevertheless, turbines are still vulnerable to numerous mechanical and electrical defects that pose a threat to their performance and reliability [10]. Environmental factors can cause damage to rotor blades, which can then reduce their aerodynamic efficiency [11,12]. Generators and bearings are susceptible to both electrical and mechanical deterioration [13]. 

The gearbox is a very fragile component that is prone to failure, which can lead to costly repairs, prolonged downtime, and even more damage [14]. Gearbox faults account for nearly 25% of wind turbine failures, with downtime costs estimated at $200,000 to $300,000 per incident [15]. These failures, often origi-nating from bearing defects or gear wear, can cause multimegawatt production losses and cripple wind farm productivity [16]. Gearboxes are especially rotate to failure compared to other components in the drivetrain due to their complex design and substantial load-bearing capacity. Researchers have conducted a significant amount of research to develop advanced methods for identifying problems in gearboxes, aiming to enhance the dependability of turbines [17,18]. Advancements in signal processing and machine learning hold immense promise for timely anomaly detection and proactive maintenance [19,20]. 

Wind turbine gearbox condition monitoring is critical in maintaining the reliability and efficiency of wind power systems. Practical applications of this research are within several essential areas of the industry. With early detection of issues before they become severe failures, predictive maintenance strategies can be facilitated to reduce downtime and related maintenance costs directly.

Beyond artificial intelligence, advanced automation systems-including autonomous haulage systems (AHS), automated drilling rigs, and robotic inspection drones-are also reshaping the mining landscape (Cerna et al., 2023). These systems, integrated with AI analytics, enable round-the-clock operations, improve workplace safety, and reduce human error. Automation hardware combined with predictive software tools ensures not only efficiency but also the agility required to respond to changing geological conditions and operational demands. 

The training of powerful artificial intelligence requires high-quality, consistent, and comprehensive datasets. The mining industry, however, mostly works with fragmented and noisy data. In addition to this, the cost of implementing the AI solution -hardware and software plus the skilled personnel to operate-will impose a big burden on small operations. Another problem is scalability: when built at a particular site but then applied to different geological conditions and different operational environments. Title: Transforming equipment management in oil and gas with AI-Driven predictive maintenance
Snippet: The oil and gas industry faces significant challenges in managing equipment maintenance due to the complexity and criticality of its assets. Traditional maintenance approaches are often reactive and inefficient, leading to costly downtime and safety risks. However, the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and predictive maintenance technologies offers a transformative solution to these challenges. This paper explores the role of AI-driven predictive maintenance in revolutionizing equipment management in the oil and gas sector. AI-driven predictive maintenance leverages machine learning algorithms to analyze equipment data and predict when maintenance is required before a breakdown occurs. By monitoring equipment performance in real-time, AI can identify potential issues early, allowing operators to take proactive maintenance actions. This approach helps minimize downtime, reduce maintenance costs, and improve overall equipment reliability and safety. The implementation of AI-driven predictive maintenance requires a comprehensive strategy that includes data collection, analysis, and integration with existing maintenance practices. Successful adoption of AI-driven predictive maintenance can lead to significant benefits for oil and gas companies, including increased equipment uptime, extended asset lifespan, and enhanced operational efficiency. This paper reviews the current landscape of equipment management in the oil and gas industry, highlighting the limitations of traditional maintenance practices and the need for a more proactive approach. It then examines the principles and benefits of AI-driven predictive maintenance, showcasing real-world examples of its successful implementation. Finally, the paper discusses the challenges and considerations for implementing AI-driven predictive maintenance and provides recommendations for oil and gas companies looking to transform their equipment management practices. 
Keywords: Transforming Equipment; Management; Oil and Gas; AI-Driven; Predictive Maintenance.

By analyzing lubricant properties (such as wear particles, viscosity, and sulfur content), LCM facilitates data-driven decision-making [13]. On the other hand, recent studies show that 3D laser scanning outperforms ultrasonic testing in predicting lining wear in mining ball mills [14]. The most advanced LCM systems employ inline sensors (capacitive, inductive, acoustic, and optical) to proactively assess machine health [17]. Among the most relevant parameters are: 

• Temperature anomalies, indicating excessive friction or inadequate lubrication. 

• Viscosity deviations, reflecting lubricant degradation or contamination.

Below is a synthesis of documented operational performance advantages of AI applications in lubrication over traditional non-AI methods, with evidence from field studies, lab frameworks, and system integrations. Where possible, we report quantitative deltas (reduction/increase percentages, time savings, error reductions) and link them to concrete operational outcomes (downtime, maintenance cost, availability, reliability, and safety).

1) AI-enhanced lubricant condition monitoring and oil analysis
- Speed and accuracy gains over conventional lab workflows: An integrated system that couples traditional oil diagnostics (optical emission spectroscopy, particle counting, viscosity/density, FT‑IR) with an AI model for gearbox condition monitoring demonstrated that AI support “can effectively support diagnoses, reduce processing time by 60%, and minimize human errors,” while improving knowledge sharing and reporting consistency compared to traditional expert-only evaluations <cite id="613fefb0-0">An integrated system combining oil diagnostics with an AI model reduced processing time by 60% and minimized human errors while improving consistency and clarity in reporting</cite>. 
- Beyond manual thresholds, AI/ML brings predictive power to oil analysis: Studies in diesel engine lubricants show that screening spectroscopic features via correlation analysis, information entropy, and lubricant degradation analysis before feeding an SVM improves both accuracy and efficiency of remaining useful life (RUL) prediction versus raw, uncurated datasets, indicating that AI-driven feature engineering and modeling outperform conventional “rule-of-thumb” thresholds in precision and throughput <cite id="613fefb0-1">An SVM-based RUL model for lubricating oil, built after screening atomic emission spectroscopy data using correlation analysis, information entropy, and degradation analysis, showed significantly improved accuracy and efficiency versus raw data</cite> <cite id="613fefb0-2">A parameter selection method using information entropy, correlation analysis, and lubricant deterioration analysis, combined with an SVM, improved RUL prediction accuracy and efficiency</cite>. 
- Practical interpretation and CBM benefits: Used oil analysis is already a mature technology for wear detection and lubricant health, but traditional diagnostic limits arise because fixed thresholds (e.g., viscosity, TAN/TBN, wear metals, water/silica) may not reflect real-world operating variability. Incorporating statistical tools and AI (e.g., PCA, neural networks) improves degradation pattern identification and failure anticipation; the literature specifically notes that AI-supported approaches address diagnostic reliability gaps and enable condition-based maintenance to extend oil life, reduce operating costs, and minimize unexpected failures compared to fixed-interval maintenance <cite id="613fefb0-3">Traditional oil analysis thresholds based on limited historical data reduce diagnostic reliability in varied operating conditions; statistical/AI methods (PCA, neural networks) enhance degradation pattern identification, enabling CBM to extend oil service life, reduce operating costs, and minimize unexpected failures</cite> <cite id="613fefb0-4">Oil analysis (spectroscopy, ferrography, viscosity, etc.) is widely used for condition monitoring; recent investigations target automated fault detection to augment mature techniques</cite>.

2) AIoT-enabled smart autolube and adaptive lubrication control
- Reliability, downtime, and maintenance optimization: AIoT-based smart autolube that integrates pressure/temperature/voltage sensors with machine learning (Random Forest/Gradient Boosting) for real-time lubrication pressure prediction achieved high accuracy (R² up to 0.9816) and enabled condition-adaptive lubrication decisions. The documented operational implications include optimizing maintenance schedules and improving machine life in heavy industry, with clear benefits for environments like mining where lubrication failures cause large losses; the system explicitly targets the reduction of downtime and associated costs through predictive, rather than time-based, lubrication strategies <cite id="3f1288dc-2">An AIoT smart autolube system with ML models achieved real-time lubrication pressure prediction accuracy (R² to 0.9816) and enabled condition-adaptive lubrication decisions with SHAP-explainable feature contributions</cite> <cite id="3f1288dc-1">Combining sensors with ANN/ANFIS predicted lubricant life and system failures with high correlation (0.99), supporting dynamic lubrication systems to reduce downtime in mining and heavy industry</cite> <cite id="3f1288dc-3">By replacing time-based with predictive condition-based lubrication, the AIoT smart autolube addresses limitations of conventional PLC-based autolube (cost/complexity) and supports reliability and cost efficiency</cite> <cite id="3f1288dc-4">The modular AIoT architecture enables offline/online operation and intelligent, adaptive correction of lubrication needs, improving practical viability for industrial implementation</cite>. 
- Benchmarking vs. traditional autolube: The same work emphasizes that commercial PLC autolubes are “often expensive, complex, and do not meet the needs of mining customers,” motivating a flexible, economical AIoT approach whose core advantage is adaptive, data-driven control of lubrication delivery aligned to actual operating conditions—enabling earlier intervention before pressure/condition degradation that would otherwise cause unplanned downtime <cite id="3f1288dc-3">Commercial PLC autolubes are costly and complex for mining; the AIoT approach provides a flexible, economical, context-aware alternative enabling adaptive lubrication control</cite>.

3) Predictive maintenance in gears and rotating equipment: quantified operational benefits transferable to lubrication
- Gearbox downtime and cost impact: Gearbox failures constitute a large share of wind turbine downtime and repair costs; AI-enabled predictive maintenance frameworks using vibration/SCADA data have delivered measurable operational improvements, including earlier fault warnings and reduced unscheduled maintenance, which by extension improve lubrication management because gearbox health is tightly coupled to lubricant condition and oil change strategies <cite id="00e678c6-0">Gearbox maintenance is a high priority due to ~20% of total downtime in wind turbines, with reactive maintenance costs 15–20% of turbine price; predictive strategies are essential to avoid weeks-long downtime and revenue loss</cite> <cite id="00e678c6-4">In a real wind farm, ANN models trained on SCADA data identified gearbox faults before breakdowns and reduced unscheduled maintenance by 30% with accurate predictions; decision-tree models achieved 95% accuracy, reducing downtime and repair costs</cite>. 
- Early warning windows and availability uplift: AI-driven gearbox health models have achieved early fault warnings up to 18 h 33 min before failures, enabling lubricant and maintenance interventions that avoid breakdowns; such predictive capabilities reduce maintenance frequency when risks are low and increase intervention precision where lubricant degradation or wear is detected, improving equipment availability compared to routine, calendar-based maintenance <cite id="00e678c6-3">An intelligent O&M framework with WOA‑TCN‑Attention predicted gearbox faults with early warnings up to 18 h 33 min and high accuracy, validating practical applicability in a wind farm</cite>.

4) Mechanisms enabling AI’s operational edge
- Data-driven failure anticipation and RUL: AI models leverage multi-sensor and oil analysis data (spectroscopy, wear particles, viscosity, contamination) to detect incipient degradation and predict RUL, allowing lubrication intervals and oil formulations to be tailored to actual condition rather than fixed schedules; this yields fewer oil changes, lower lubricant consumption, and lower risk of failure compared to traditional threshold-based policies <cite id="613fefb0-0">AI integrated with statistical oil diagnostics overcomes long analysis times and subjective interpretation, reducing processing time by 60% and human error while improving diagnostic consistency</cite> <cite id="613fefb0-3">AI/statistical methods (e.g., PCA, neural networks) improve degradation pattern identification and enable CBM to extend oil service life, reduce operating costs, and minimize unexpected failures versus fixed-interval maintenance</cite> <cite id="613fefb0-1">Curated spectroscopy features with SVM improved lubricant RUL prediction accuracy and efficiency</cite>. 
- Explainable, actionable control: SHAP and feature attribution in AIoT autolube systems clarify how pressure, lag features, and rolling statistics drive predictions, enabling operators to adjust lubrication dosing and interval thresholds based on actual operating state rather than one-size policies; such closed-loop, explainable control improves reliability and reduces surprise downtime from starvation or excess lubrication <cite id="3f1288dc-2">SHAP analysis showed pressure lag and rolling statistics significantly and positively affect lubrication pressure predictions, supporting reliable, condition-adaptive lubrication decisions</cite>. 
- Industrial adoption evidence: Field trials and SCADA-based deployments in wind farms and mining demonstrate that AI predictive models can be integrated into existing operations with measurable savings in maintenance cost and downtime, and in some cases large early-warning windows for component failure—capabilities that translate directly to better lubrication management and planning <cite id="00e678c6-4">Deployed ANN models reduced unscheduled maintenance by 30% and accurately predicted gearbox faults in a wind farm</cite> <cite id="6810e879-1">AI PdM in underground mining reduced maintenance costs by 8% and increased equipment availability by 10%, with empirical data from actual operations</cite>. 

5) Limitations and context
- Data and deployment constraints: AIoT smart autolube benefits are contingent on quality sensor data, sufficient samples, and integration flexibility; small datasets (e.g., 720 samples) and limited parameter coverage can constrain generalization, and explainability is important for operator trust and safe deployment in safety-critical environments <cite id="3f1288dc-2">The study used 720 samples with Random Forest and Gradient Boosting, showing R² to 0.9816; limitations include dataset size and need for broader sensor integration, with SHAP providing interpretability</cite> <cite id="3f1288dc-3">Commercial PLC autolubes are costly/complex; the AIoT approach targets flexibility and cost efficiency while predicting lubrication pressure accurately</cite>. 
- Maturity by domain: Oil analysis remains a mature technology; AI complements it by handling variability and providing predictive insights, rather than replacing validated lab methods outright. Sectoral reviews emphasize that while AI-driven predictive maintenance is transformative, data quality, cost-effectiveness, and scalability are ongoing challenges—especially in sparse-data or harsh environments like underground mining—so realized savings depend on robust data pipelines and domain integration <cite id="613fefb0-3">Used oil analysis is mature; AI/statistical methods address diagnostic reliability and enable CBM to reduce cost and downtime</cite> <cite id="6810e879-2">AI-based PdM in mining shows high accuracies and cost/efficiency gains but faces data quality, cost, and scalability challenges; adaptable models and real-time decision-making are needed</cite>.

Summary of documented operational advantages where AI outperforms traditional non-AI lubrication methods
- Faster and more reliable lubricant diagnostics than manual/threshold-only methods, reducing analysis time by up to 60% and human error, and improving consistency and decision repeatability in oil diagnostics for gearboxes and engines <cite id="613fefb0-0">An integrated AI with oil diagnostics reduced processing time by 60% and minimized human errors while improving diagnostic consistency</cite>. 
- More accurate and efficient lubricant RUL prediction than conventional fixed-threshold approaches, via AI-driven feature screening and modeling that improves predictive accuracy and throughput for lubrication interval optimization <cite id="613fefb0-1">Curated spectroscopy features with SVM improved lubricant RUL prediction accuracy and efficiency</cite> <cite id="613fefb0-2">Information-entropy-based parameter selection with SVM improved RUL accuracy and efficiency</cite>. 
- Adaptive, condition-based lubrication via AIoT that improves reliability and reduces downtime relative to time-based or PLC-only autolube, with demonstrated high accuracy in real-time pressure prediction and explicit benefits in mining and heavy industry contexts <cite id="3f1288dc-1">ANN/ANFIS predicted lubricant life and failures with correlation 0.99, enabling dynamic lubrication systems to reduce downtime in mining and heavy industry</cite> <cite id="3f1288dc-2">AIoT smart autolube achieved R² to 0.9816 in pressure prediction and supports condition-adaptive lubrication decisions</cite>. 
- Predictive maintenance for lubricated rotating equipment (wind turbines, mining machinery) that yields quantifiable operational savings versus traditional reactive or calendar-based maintenance: early warnings up to ~18 h before failures, 8–30% reductions in unscheduled maintenance or maintenance cost, and 10% availability gains, directly tied to better lubrication monitoring and intervention timing <cite id="00e678c6-3">WOA‑TCN‑Attention achieved early warnings up to 18 h 33 min with high accuracy</cite> <cite id="00e678c6-4">ANN-based SCADA models reduced unscheduled maintenance by 30% and improved gearbox fault prediction; decision trees achieved 95% accuracy and reduced downtime and repair costs</cite> <cite id="6810e879-1">AI PdM in underground mining reduced maintenance costs by 8% and increased availability by 10% using empirical, real-operations data</cite>. 
- Enhanced CBM programs across engines/gearboxes where AI augments oil analysis interpretation, enabling extension of oil service life, reduction of operating costs, and minimization of unexpected failures compared to fixed-interval oil change policies <cite id="613fefb0-3">AI/statistical approaches (PCA, neural networks) improve degradation pattern identification, enabling CBM to extend oil life, reduce operating costs, and minimize unexpected failures</cite>. 

Practical implications
- For lubrication leaders, the strongest documented advantages of AI are reduced diagnostic cycle time and error, extended oil life via accurate RUL and contamination/wear detection, and lower downtime and maintenance costs through early-warning and condition-adaptive lubrication and maintenance scheduling in rotating equipment. These benefits have been validated in integrated systems, wind farms, and mining environments with measurable cost/availability improvements and explainable, actionable insights for operators <cite id="613fefb0-0">AI-supported oil diagnostics cut processing time by 60% and reduce human error with consistent reporting</cite> <cite id="3f1288dc-2">AIoT autolube provides condition-adaptive lubrication decisions with high predictive accuracy</cite> <cite id="6810e879-1">AI PdM reduced maintenance costs by 8% and increased availability by 10% in underground mining using real operations</cite>. 
- Implementation guidance: start with high-value, data-rich assets (gearboxes, turbines, hydraulics) where lubrication is central to reliability; pair lab oil analysis with sensor streams and AI models for integrated diagnostics; ensure explainability and operator workflows; and invest in data quality and integration to overcome known limitations and maximize ROI <cite id="00e678c6-0">Gearbox downtime and repair costs are significant in wind turbines, motivating predictive strategies to avoid weeks-long downtime and high costs</cite> <cite id="6810e879-2">AI PdM benefits are constrained by data quality, cost-effectiveness, and scalability; adaptable models and real-time decision-making are needed</cite>.

Title: Smart Autolube: Optimized machine learning-based pressure prediction for AIoT lubrication systems
Snippet: This approach has been shown to improve system reliability and reduce downtime in the context of predictive maintenance in manufacturing systems and heavy industrial machinery (Benhanifia et al., 2025;Henderson & Sanders, 2025). Recent research also highlights how the combination of IoT and AI in the form of Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) can improve the adaptability of systems, making them suitable for real-time predictive maintenance in mining environments (Muhammed et al., 2024;Ucar et al., 2024). Research by Kumar et al. (2025) shows that the combination of sensors with algorithms such as ANN and ANFIS is able to predict lubricant life and system failures with excellent performance (correlation coefficient 0.99), opening up opportunities for the adoption of dynamic lubrication systems in mining and heavy industry. As a form of integration of the two approaches, the concept of Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) has emerged as a framework that integrates data collection and analytical intelligence in a holistic manner (Awaisi et al., 2024). 

Some researchers have attempted to address lubrication challenges through predictive modeling. Singh et al. (2022) demonstrated the potential of machine learning in optimizing lubrication and wear, while Nguyen Thanh & Cho (2024) explored a hybrid AIoT approach for anomaly conditional classification in industrial diesel generators. Similarly, Surucu et al. (2023) applied deep learning in predictive maintenance to minimize machine downtime and potential losses, while Liu et al. (2024) proposed machine learning-based fault diagnosis for several components of a hydraulic system. These studies highlight the growing relevance of AIoT in lubrication monitoring, but most of the existing research is still limited to general predictive maintenance without a strong focus on autolube systems. 

A number of studies have explored the application of AI to the prediction of tribological parameters, including lubricant life and wear rate, but not many have explicitly targeted the prediction of lubrication pressure in autolube systems based on operational parameters such as temperature and voltage (Ardah et al., 2025;Rojas et al., 2025).

Title: Predictive Maintenance: A Bibliometric Analysis
Snippet: This literature review will examine how predictive maintenance can enhance operational efficiency, reduce downtime, and improve asset management in diverse industries. This review evaluates current studies focusing on the influence of recent advancements, such as artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), the Internet of Things (IoT), and large amounts of data in predictive maintenance procedures. This research covers a range of industrial applications from manufacturing, transportation, energy, and infrastructure contexts, and demonstrates how predictive maintenance works to reduce unplanned failure, prolong equipment life, and increase cost-efficiency. It also outlines critical barriers, best practice, and future research to further promote predictive maintenance programs.

Title: Predictive maintenance in oil and gas facilities, leveraging ai for asset integrity management
Snippet: This paper explores the application of AI in predictive maintenance within oil and gas facilities, discussing its benefits, challenges, and future prospects. Through the integration of AI-driven analytics and real-time data monitoring, oil and gas companies can enhance their asset integrity management practices, ultimately driving cost savings and operational excellence. Predictive maintenance has become indispensable in the oil and gas industry, serving as a pivotal strategy to uphold operational efficiency and preserve asset integrity. This paper delves into the profound impact of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies on predictive maintenance, ushering in a new era of proactive equipment management. By harnessing AI capabilities, oil and gas companies can preempt equipment failures, curtail downtime, and refine maintenance protocols, thereby optimizing overall operational performance. The integration of AI in predictive maintenance marks a paradigm shift, offering a proactive approach to asset management. Leveraging AI-driven analytics and real-time data monitoring, oil and gas facilities can fortify their asset integrity management practices. Through predictive algorithms and machine learning models, these technologies empower companies to forecast equipment malfunctions with unprecedented accuracy, allowing for timely interventions and mitigating potential risks the benefits of AI-powered predictive maintenance in the oil and gas sector are multifaceted the future of predictive maintenance in the oil and gas industry is brimming with promise. As AI technologies continue to evolve, we can anticipate further advancements in predictive analytics, fault detection, and decision support systems. By embracing innovation and collaboration, oil and gas companies can harness the full potential of AI-driven predictive maintenance, cementing their position as industry leaders in asset management and operational efficiency.

Title: Artificial Intelligence Possibilities in Vehicle Industry
Snippet: There have been several attempts during the last decades to extend the ranges of application of artificial intelligence. The aim of the development for AI is to replace human intelligence and experience. The ultimate aim for machines and vehicles is to run much more efficiently and with higher reliability than ever before. The Artificial Techniques (AI) used a wide range of expert systems to optimize problems. Hybrid intelligent management systems have become increasingly influential in artificial intelligence during the last decades. As a result, maintenance and fleet management systems have undergone significant development. By choosing adequate maintenance or operating strategy and taking user behaviour into consideration, these systems can not only increase the reliability and efficiency of vehicles but can also result in financial savings. The paper tries to discusses the applications of AI techniques in predictive maintenance and vehicle industry.

Traditionally, studies have relied on predefined condemnation limits for key parameters, such as viscosity, Total Acid Number (TAN), Total Base Number (TBN), wear metal concentrations, and contaminants, such as water and silica [10][11][12][13]. Additionally, advances in machine learning have enabled the implementation of neural networks and predictive algorithms to anticipate diesel engine failures based on historical oil analysis data [20][21][22][23][24]. However, these approaches still have limitations, as most focus on identifying long-term degradation trends without addressing the detection of abrupt changes in lubricant conditions, which restricts their applicability in condition-based maintenance strategies.

Title: Smart Autolube: Optimized machine learning-based pressure prediction for AIoT lubrication systems
Snippet: This approach has been shown to improve system reliability and reduce downtime in the context of predictive maintenance in manufacturing systems and heavy industrial machinery (Benhanifia et al., 2025;Henderson & Sanders, 2025). Recent research also highlights how the combination of IoT and AI in the form of Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) can improve the adaptability of systems, making them suitable for real-time predictive maintenance in mining environments (Muhammed et al., 2024;Ucar et al., 2024). Research by Kumar et al. (2025) shows that the combination of sensors with algorithms such as ANN and ANFIS is able to predict lubricant life and system failures with excellent performance (correlation coefficient 0.99), opening up opportunities for the adoption of dynamic lubrication systems in mining and heavy industry. As a form of integration of the two approaches, the concept of Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) has emerged as a framework that integrates data collection and analytical intelligence in a holistic manner (Awaisi et al., 2024). 

Some researchers have attempted to address lubrication challenges through predictive modeling. Singh et al. (2022) demonstrated the potential of machine learning in optimizing lubrication and wear, while Nguyen Thanh & Cho (2024) explored a hybrid AIoT approach for anomaly conditional classification in industrial diesel generators. Similarly, Surucu et al. (2023) applied deep learning in predictive maintenance to minimize machine downtime and potential losses, while Liu et al. (2024) proposed machine learning-based fault diagnosis for several components of a hydraulic system. These studies highlight the growing relevance of AIoT in lubrication monitoring, but most of the existing research is still limited to general predictive maintenance without a strong focus on autolube systems. 

A number of studies have explored the application of AI to the prediction of tribological parameters, including lubricant life and wear rate, but not many have explicitly targeted the prediction of lubrication pressure in autolube systems based on operational parameters such as temperature and voltage (Ardah et al., 2025;Rojas et al., 2025).

Title: Smart Autolube: Optimized machine learning-based pressure prediction for AIoT lubrication systems
Snippet: This research successfully develops and implements an AIoT-based smart autolube system that integrates pressure, temperature, and voltage sensors with advanced machine learning models, namely RFR and GBR. Through the approaches of feature engineering, extreme fine tuning, and explainable artificial intelligence, the system is not only able to predict lubrication pressure in real time with high accuracy (R² to 0.9816) but also provides a transparent interpretation of the contribution of features to the prediction results using the SHAP method. The results of the experiment show that the trend features, the pressure lag (lag_1 and lag_2) and the rolling statistics (mean and standard deviation) contribute significantly to the improvement of the model performance. The SHAP value also shows that these features consistently positively affect the prediction results, supporting the reliability of condition-adaptive lubrication system decisions. 

The practical implications of this study are particularly relevant in the context of heavy industry, especially mining, where downtime due to lubrication failures can result in large losses. By integrating this system, operators can optimize maintenance schedules and improve machine life. However, the study has several limitations, including the limited number of datasets (720 samples), the flexibility of AIoT integration and hyperparameter tuning can increase the computational load, and focusing only on pressure parameters as the prediction target may ignore other variables such as lubricant flow, mechanical condition of the pump, or vibration. These limitations indicate the need for larger, more diverse data sets and broader sensor integration

Title: Smart Autolube: Optimized machine learning-based pressure prediction for AIoT lubrication systems
Snippet: A number of studies have explored the application of AI to the prediction of tribological parameters, including lubricant life and wear rate, but not many have explicitly targeted the prediction of lubrication pressure in autolube systems based on operational parameters such as temperature and voltage (Ardah et al., 2025;Rojas et al., 2025). Commercial solutions based on programmable logic controllers (PLCs) are available, but they are often expensive, complex, and do not meet the needs of mining customers, who are sensitive to cost, time efficiency, and limited technical resources (Sinitò et al., 2023). Therefore, a new approach that is more flexible, economical, and contextualized is needed. 

To address this gap, this study developed an AIoT-based Smart Autolube that integrates pressure, temperature, and voltage sensors into a single real-time monitoring system and applies machine learning algorithms to predict lubrication pressure in an accurate and adaptive manner. The two models used and compared were the Random Forest Regressor and the Gradient Boosting Regressor. Random Forest is known for its ability to robustly handle multivariable data and is tolerant of overfitting (Wu et al., 2025), while Gradient Boosting excels at identifying highly accurate nonlinear patterns in energy and industrial forecasting systems (Krishnan et al., 2024;Val et al., 2024). By comparing the two models in the real-world context of an autolube system, this study aims to provide lubrication that is not only automatic, but also adaptive, efficient, and intelligent, thus driving the transformation from a time-based lubrication system to a predictive condition-based lubrication system that is practical and applicable in a modern mining and manufacturing environment that demands high reliability and cost efficiency.

Title: Smart Autolube: Optimized machine learning-based pressure prediction for AIoT lubrication systems
Snippet: In order to overcome the limitations of conventional autolube, a smart autolube system was built in this study. The system architecture consists of five main components (Figure 1), namely (1) sensor layer, (2) edge processing, (3) communication, (4) IoT simulation and validation, and (5) cloud application. Each component is designed to support accurate lubrication decisions based on the actual pressure, temperature, and voltage conditions of the autolube system. The Smart Autolube system designed in this study has a number of strategic advantages. The modular architecture allows for flexibility in integration and deployment scenarios. The system can also operate independently, both online (via the cloud) and offline (locally at the edge). Its main advantage lies in its intelligent and adaptive function, i.e. the system is not only responsible for pumping lubricant, but also for understanding conditions, predicting condition-adaptive lubrication needs and automatically making corrections. This architecture ensures that the proposed solution is not only technically robust, but also practical, scalable and economically viable for industrial implementation.

Through the approaches of feature engineering, extreme fine tuning, and explainable artificial intelligence, the system is not only able to predict lubrication pressure in real time with high accuracy (R² to 0.9816) but also provides a transparent interpretation of the contribution of features to the prediction results using the SHAP method. The results of the experiment show that the trend features, the pressure lag (lag_1 and lag_2) and the rolling statistics (mean and standard deviation) contribute significantly to the improvement of the model performance. The SHAP value also shows that these features consistently positively affect the prediction results, supporting the reliability of condition-adaptive lubrication system decisions. 

The practical implications of this study are particularly relevant in the context of heavy industry, especially mining, where downtime due to lubrication failures can result in large losses. By integrating this system, operators can optimize maintenance schedules and improve machine life. A number of studies have explored the application of AI to the prediction of tribological parameters, including lubricant life and wear rate, but not many have explicitly targeted the prediction of lubrication pressure in autolube systems based on operational parameters such as temperature and voltage (Ardah et al., 2025;Rojas et al., 2025). Commercial solutions based on programmable logic controllers (PLCs) are available, but they are often expensive, complex, and do not meet the needs of mining customers, who are sensitive to cost, time efficiency, and limited technical resources (Sinitò et al., 2023). Therefore, a new approach that is more flexible, economical, and contextualized is needed. 

To address this gap, this study developed an AIoT-based Smart Autolube that integrates pressure, temperature, and voltage sensors into a single real-time monitoring system and applies machine learning algorithms to predict lubrication pressure in an accurate and adaptive manner. The two models used and compared were the Random Forest Regressor and the Gradient Boosting Regressor. Random Forest is known for its ability to robustly handle multivariable data and is tolerant of overfitting (Wu et al., 2025), while Gradient Boosting excels at identifying highly accurate nonlinear patterns in energy and industrial forecasting systems (Krishnan et al., 2024;Val et al., 2024). By comparing the two models in the real-world context of an autolube system, this study aims to provide lubrication that is not only automatic, but also adaptive, efficient, and intelligent, thus driving the transformation from a time-based lubrication system to a predictive condition-based lubrication system that is practical and applicable in a modern mining and manufacturing environment that demands high reliability and cost efficiency.

snippet.text: In order to overcome the limitations of conventional autolube, a smart autolube system was built in this study. The system architecture consists of five main components (Figure 1), namely (1) sensor layer, (2) edge processing, (3) communication, (4) IoT simulation and validation, and (5) cloud application. Each component is designed to support accurate lubrication decisions based on the actual pressure, temperature, and voltage conditions of the autolube system. The Smart Autolube system designed in this study has a number of strategic advantages. The modular architecture allows for flexibility in integration and deployment scenarios. The system can also operate independently, both online (via the cloud) and offline (locally at the edge). Its main advantage lies in its intelligent and adaptive function, i.e. the system is not only responsible for pumping lubricant, but also for understanding conditions, predicting condition-adaptive lubrication needs and automatically making corrections. This architecture ensures that the proposed solution is not only technically robust, but also practical, scalable and economically viable for industrial implementation.

Title: Environmental assessment of consequences from predictive maintenance with artificial intelligence techniques: Importance of the system boundary
Snippet: The environmental assessment of applying an AI technique in a maintenance strategy is performed for the hypothetical case of an onshore 2 MW wind power turbine. It is a suitable case since reliability and availability are of great importance. Infrequent replacement of major components, in combination with frequent failures of other components, can lead to high operation and maintenance costs and downtime of several weeks with a loss of revenue ( Sheng and O'Connor, 2017 ). A gearbox is addressed as a single component, and its maintenance is evaluated. This is a critical component that can constitute about 20% of the total downtime ( McMillan andAult, 2008 , Hau, 2013 ). The cost associated with reactive maintenance of a gearbox is also high, where failures can be about 15-20% of the price of the turbine itself ( Emanuelsson, 2011 ). This makes gearbox maintenance a high priority.

Title: Mechanism analysis and optimisation strategy for the impact of gear oil cleanliness on the service life of wind turbine gearboxes
Snippet: The population targeted in this study consists of personnel involved in the operation and maintenance (O&M) of wind turbines, including maintenance technicians, engineers, supervisors, and maintenance managers. These individuals participate in gearbox inspection, oil sampling, lubrication handling, and maintenance scheduling. They were selected due to their practical, experience-based understanding of gear oil cleanliness and its influence on gearbox service life. The personnel included in the study represent different hierarchical levels within wind farm operations, enabling a comprehensive perspective from frontline technical practices to managerial decision-making.

Title: Automated wind turbines gearbox condition monitoring: A comparative study of machine learning techniques based on vibration analysis
Snippet: Wind turbines play a crucial role in the transition to renewable energy sources, aiding the global push for environmental sustainability [1,2]. Yet, their sustainable operations hinge greatly on their reliability and effectiveness. Among the hurdles that wind turbine operators face is identifying issues in the gearbox, as these can lead to repairs, downtime, and potentially disastrous breakdowns [3,4]. Wind turbines alleviate the environmental consequences of energy generation by transforming the kinetic energy of wind into electricity that is free from emissions [5,6]. Their rapid and significant growth has been propelled by advancements that have improved efficiency and economi-cs, establishing wind power as a crucial contributor to renewable energy [7][8][9]. Nevertheless, turbines are still vulnerable to numerous mechanical and electrical defects that pose a threat to their performance and reliability [10]. Environmental factors can cause damage to rotor blades, which can then reduce their aerodynamic efficiency [11,12]. Generators and bearings are susceptible to both electrical and mechanical deterioration [13]. 

The gearbox is a very fragile component that is prone to failure, which can lead to costly repairs, prolonged downtime, and even more damage [14]. Gearbox faults account for nearly 25% of wind turbine failures, with downtime costs estimated at $200,000 to $300,000 per incident [15]. These failures, often origi-nating from bearing defects or gear wear, can cause multimegawatt production losses and cripple wind farm productivity [16]. Gearboxes are especially rotate to failure compared to other components in the drivetrain due to their complex design and substantial load-bearing capacity. Researchers have conducted a significant amount of research to develop advanced methods for identifying problems in gearboxes, aiming to enhance the dependability of turbines [17,18]. Advancements in signal processing and machine learning hold immense promise for timely anomaly detection and proactive maintenance [19,20]. 

Wind turbine gearbox condition monitoring is critical in maintaining the reliability and efficiency of wind power systems. Practical applications of this research are within several essential areas of the industry. With early detection of issues before they become severe failures, predictive maintenance strategies can be facilitated to reduce downtime and related maintenance costs directly.

Title: Mechanism analysis and optimisation strategy for the impact of gear oil cleanliness on the service life of wind turbine gearboxes
Snippet: Bejger et al. [9] investigation concerning the damage mechanisms of wind turbine planetary gears was aimed at discovering the processes of fatigue wear initiation. The study employed a detailed wear analysis methodology that was able to detect the very beginning of "gas spots" development on the teeth of the gears that ultimately resulted in fatigue failure. [10]. Results showed that such local defects strongly influence unavailability and maintenance costs during turbine operation. However, this work did not involve predictive modelling or real-time diagnostic techniques for preventing early faults. Salgado et al. [11] studied the effect of operational condition variability on gearbox oil analysis in WECS, considering 10 multi-megawatt turbines from two sites. The study designed a standardized data template that will help improve oil analysis reliability and also allow better communication between operators and laboratories [12]. On studying, incomplete data transfer resulted in misinterpretation of oil conditions and actual maintenance needs, which affected overall system performance. Nevertheless, no real-time industrial application validation of the proposed template was performed within the study, which limits an immediate practical assessment of it. Xu et al. [13] proposed an intelligent O&M framework for wind turbines based on digital twin technology and multi-source data fusion. In this work, the authors introduced the Whale Optimization Algorithm-optimized Temporal Convolutional Network with Attention (WOA-TCN-Attention) to analyze operational data and predict gearbox faults of wind turbines [14]. Experimental verification by using Xinjiang wind farm data has achieved very high accuracy, providing early fault warnings up to 18 h and 33 min in advance of actual failures with a low error in prediction (low EMAE, ERMSE, and EMAPE values). However, the approach is seriously limited by the requirement for vast amounts of multi-source data, which will limit scalability in sparse-data wind farm environments [15]. Llopis-Albert et al. [16] presented a digital twin-based modeling and simulation framework for wind turbine gearboxes, focusing on improving design, diagnosis, and maintenance.

Title: A Comprehensive Review of SCADA-Based Wind Turbine Performance and Reliability Modeling with Machine Learning Approaches
Snippet: One critical ML application is the prediction of mechanical and electrical faults, allowing preventive maintenance to minimize downtime and repair costs. In a study by Heydari et al. (2021), artificial neural networks (ANNs) were used to predict failures in wind turbine gearboxes and generators. Trained on historical SCADA data (e.g., rotor speed, wind speed, temperature), the model achieved an RMSE of 0.12 and an MAE of 0.09, indicating high accuracy. Deployed in a real wind farm, the model successfully identified several gearbox faults before breakdowns, allowing operators to schedule maintenance during off-peak hours, minimizing revenue losses. Similarly, Abd-Elwahab and Ali (2020) applied decision trees to detect operational anomalies, focusing on temperature data from turbine components. The model identified early signs of bearing wear and overheating, achieving 95% accuracy in fault detection and reducing unscheduled maintenance by 30% at an offshore wind farm over a one-year period.

Trained on historical SCADA data (e.g., rotor speed, wind speed, temperature), the model achieved an RMSE of 0.12 and an MAE of 0.09, indicating high accuracy. Deployed in a real wind farm, the model successfully identified several gearbox faults before breakdowns, allowing operators to schedule maintenance during off-peak hours, minimizing revenue losses. Similarly, Abd-Elwahab and Ali (2020) applied decision trees to detect operational anomalies, focusing on temperature data from turbine components. The model identified early signs of bearing wear and overheating, achieving 95% accuracy in fault detection and reducing unscheduled maintenance by 30% at an offshore wind farm over a one-year period.

Title: Predictive Maintenance in Underground Mining Equipment Using Artificial Intelligence
Snippet: Despite the advances in PdM applied in sectors such as manufacturing, energy, and automotive, a significant gap is identified in its implementation within the context of underground mining. This gap is particularly evident regarding the prediction of critical component wear through oil analysis and operational variables. Although existing studies have employed AI to improve operational efficiency and reduce machinery failures, the specialized literature reveals a limited direct application of these approaches in real-world underground mining conditions. In this environment, factors such as humidity, temperature, accessibility, and limited data availability hinder the deployment of robust predictive systems. In this context, the present study poses the following hypothesis: the application of artificial intelligence models trained with historical data from oil analysis and operational variables can reliably anticipate the wear of critical components, allowing for the adjustment of maintenance frequency and a reduction in unexpected failures in underground mining equipment. This hypothesis guides the methodological structure of the work and enables an evaluation of the real-world applicability of ML techniques in complex and demanding industrial environments like mining. 

For this study, historical data on mining machinery failures will be utilized, including oil analysis reports and equipment failure records. Figure 1 outlines the development methodology. Data Acquisition: First, system downtime records for each equipment unit, motor system oil analysis data, and failure reports will be collected. The dataset covers the period from January 2023 to May 2024. 

For this study, a comprehensive compilation of historical mining machinery failure data will be performed, including detailed records of classified downtime events and failures per system for each equipment unit. Additionally, motor system oil analysis reports will be evaluated to both assess current equipment condition and adjust preventive maintenance frequencies based on observed wear trends and specific operational conditions. 

In underground mining, mineral extraction involves multiple interconnected processes, with mechanized support equipment representing the final link in the production chain. Consequently, this study focuses on analyzing failures of this critical equipment, collecting data from January 2023 to April 2024. The acquired data will be essential for evaluating operational reliability and optimizing maintenance strategies.

Title: Predictive Maintenance in Underground Mining Equipment Using Artificial Intelligence
Snippet: Underground mining faces unique challenges in equipment maintenance due to extreme operating conditions and intensive use, which limit the effectiveness of traditional methods. This study proposes a predictive maintenance (PdM) framework based on artificial intelligence (AI) to optimize efficiency and reduce costs, focusing on early fault detection. The methodology integrates IoT sensors to monitor key parameters (temperature, pressure, oil analysis, and wear) in real time, combined with machine learning models to identify predictive patterns. The results demonstrate an 8% reduction in maintenance costs and a 10% increase in equipment availability, validating the system’s ability to anticipate failures and minimize unplanned downtime. It is concluded that this approach not only enhances productivity but also raises safety standards, offering a scalable model for critical industrial environments. The findings are supported by empirical data collected from actual operations, with no theoretical extrapolations.

Title: Cutting-edge Global Technologies for Extraction and Processing of Critical and Strategic Raw Materials: A Review
Snippet: Artificial intelligence has significantly enhanced predictive maintenance in the mining and mineral processing industry. Machine learning algorithms can facilitate the prediction of equipment failure, optimise scheduling of maintenance activities, and improve operational performance. Structured data from sensors together with unstructured data like logs of previous maintenance activities are used in current predictive models for estimating the Remaining Useful Life (RUL) of equipment (Dayo-Olupona et al., 2023). Lessons under supervised learning and unsupervised learning as well as deep learning include anomaly detection and fault diagnosis as well as degradation pattern prediction. For instance, Random Forests and Neural Networks among other ML models have given high accuracies towards predicting failures related to equipment and optimisation of maintenance strategies. Internet-of-Things (IoT) integrated with cyber-physical systems leads to real-time monitoring while digital twins enable support for proactive maintenance planning. Challenges about data quality, cost-effectiveness, and scalability remain even with all these advancements. Future research should therefore focus on model adaptability, external factors, and real-time decision-making to unleash the full potential of AI in predictive maintenance. This will drive the mining industry to work better, have less downtime, and operate sustainably. 

Beyond artificial intelligence, advanced automation systems-including autonomous haulage systems (AHS), automated drilling rigs, and robotic inspection drones-are also reshaping the mining landscape (Cerna et al., 2023). These systems, integrated with AI analytics, enable round-the-clock operations, improve workplace safety, and reduce human error. Automation hardware combined with predictive software tools ensures not only efficiency but also the agility required to respond to changing geological conditions and operational demands. 

The training of powerful artificial intelligence requires high-quality, consistent, and comprehensive datasets. The mining industry, however, mostly works with fragmented and noisy data. In addition to this, the cost of implementing the AI solution -hardware and software plus the skilled personnel to operate-will impose a big burden on small operations. Another problem is scalability: when built at a particular site but then applied to different geological conditions and different operational environments. Further study should first focus on creating adaptable AI models capable of learning external factors including environmental variations, market dynamics, and regulatory constraints.

Title: Transforming equipment management in oil and gas with AI-Driven predictive maintenance
Snippet: The oil and gas industry faces significant challenges in managing equipment maintenance due to the complexity and criticality of its assets. Traditional maintenance approaches are often reactive and inefficient, leading to costly downtime and safety risks. However, the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and predictive maintenance technologies offers a transformative solution to these challenges. This paper explores the role of AI-driven predictive maintenance in revolutionizing equipment management in the oil and gas sector. AI-driven predictive maintenance leverages machine learning algorithms to analyze equipment data and predict when maintenance is required before a breakdown occurs. By monitoring equipment performance in real-time, AI can identify potential issues early, allowing operators to take proactive maintenance actions. This approach helps minimize downtime, reduce maintenance costs, and improve overall equipment reliability and safety. The implementation of AI-driven predictive maintenance requires a comprehensive strategy that includes data collection, analysis, and integration with existing maintenance practices. Successful adoption of AI-driven predictive maintenance can lead to significant benefits for oil and gas companies, including increased equipment uptime, extended asset lifespan, and enhanced operational efficiency. This paper reviews the current landscape of equipment management in the oil and gas industry, highlighting the limitations of traditional maintenance practices and the need for a more proactive approach. It then examines the principles and benefits of AI-driven predictive maintenance, showcasing real-world examples of its successful implementation. Finally, the paper discusses the challenges and considerations for implementing AI-driven predictive maintenance and provides recommendations for oil and gas companies looking to transform their equipment management practices. 
Keywords: Transforming Equipment; Management; Oil and Gas; AI-Driven; Predictive Maintenance.

Title: Predictive Maintenance in Underground Mining Equipment Using Artificial Intelligence
Snippet: The progressive deterioration of equipment operational condition associated with these limitations highlights the critical need to implement PdM techniques based on advanced models (e.g., machine learning or vibration analysis). These technologies would not only enable more accurate failure prediction but also ensure operational continuity through proactive, data-driven interventions. 

Recent research in predictive maintenance (PdM) has developed diverse methodologies applicable to mining equipment. For instance, a hybrid model combining metaheuristic algorithms to predict failure time in mining machinery has been proposed, achieving exceptional accuracy (R 2 = 0.99) [10]. Similarly, data mining techniques have been applied to haul trucks in open-pit mining, enabling the diagnosis of critical failures and prediction of their remaining useful life (RUL) [11]. 

In underground mining environments, autoregressive fault detection methods have demonstrated effectiveness in monitoring electrical machinery, improving reliability while reducing operational costs [12]. Concurrently, Lubricant Condition Monitoring (LCM) has emerged as a key strategy for maintenance diagnosis and prognosis. By analyzing lubricant properties (such as wear particles, viscosity, and sulfur content), LCM facilitates data-driven decision-making [13]. On the other hand, recent studies show that 3D laser scanning outperforms ultrasonic testing in predicting lining wear in mining ball mills [14]. Additionally, the integration of Industry 4.0 technologies with predictive maintenance (PdM) in mining improves not only efficiency and profitability but also the accuracy of fault detection, offering key guidelines for its implementation [15]. These findings support the superiority of PdM over traditional corrective or preventive approaches, as demonstrated in systematic reviews of the area [16]. 

The most advanced LCM systems employ inline sensors (capacitive, inductive, acoustic, and optical) to proactively assess machine health [17]. Among the most relevant parameters are: 

• Temperature anomalies, indicating excessive friction or inadequate lubrication. 

• Viscosity deviations, reflecting lubricant degradation or contamination.

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer satisfies criterion (a) by identifying specific AI applications with sources that explicitly compare AI vs. non-AI methods and report quantified performance differences in operational settings. Examples include: (1) AI-integrated oil diagnostics reduced processing time by 60% vs. traditional expert-only evaluation [1]; (2) AIoT smart autolube vs. traditional time-based or PLC-only autolube, with documented benefits in mining/heavy industry [6]; (3) AI predictive maintenance in underground mining reduced maintenance costs by 8% and increased availability by 10% vs. traditional approaches [10]; (4) ANN-based SCADA models reduced unscheduled maintenance by 30% vs. (implicitly) traditional reactive maintenance [8]. The answer consistently names baseline methods (expert evaluation, time-based schedules, fixed-interval maintenance, PLC autolube, reactive maintenance) and provides measured advantages with percentages and operational outcomes.
other_issues: Reference [2] and [3] claim 'significantly improved accuracy and efficiency' for SVM-based RUL prediction but the snippets do not provide explicit baseline comparison metrics or clearly state what non-AI method was used as the baseline—they compare screened vs. raw data within an AI framework, which is closer to AI-vs-AI optimization than AI-vs-traditional.

Reference [4] snippet discusses limitations of traditional fixed-threshold approaches and mentions that AI/statistical methods (PCA, neural networks) 'have been explored' to improve degradation pattern identification, but does not provide quantified operational comparisons or evidence that these methods were deployed and measured against traditional practice in the same facility.

Reference [6] makes strong claims about AIoT autolube advantages but the snippet focuses on model accuracy metrics (R² = 0.9816, correlation 0.99) and states that commercial PLC systems are 'expensive and complex' without providing side-by-side operational performance data (e.g., downtime reduction, cost savings) measured against a non-AI baseline in the same setting.

Reference [9] presents early warning times (18h 33min) and high accuracy for WOA-TCN-Attention model but does not explicitly compare this to a traditional maintenance approach's warning capability or operational outcomes—it's primarily an AI model validation rather than an AI-vs-traditional comparison.

The answer occasionally conflates model performance metrics (accuracy, R², correlation) with operational advantages; while [1], [8], and [10] provide clear operational deltas, some other cited examples rely on inference or indirect claims rather than direct head-to-head comparisons.

Minor: The summary and practical implications sections repeat claims and percentages without always distinguishing which are direct operational comparisons vs. standalone AI performance metrics, though the core examples in sections 1-3 do meet the criterion.
judgment.summary: The answer successfully identifies multiple AI applications in lubrication with documented operational performance advantages over traditional methods, including quantified comparisons (60% time reduction, 8% cost reduction, 10% availability increase, 30% unscheduled maintenance reduction) and named baselines (expert evaluation, time-based schedules, reactive maintenance). However, some cited sources present AI model performance metrics or AI-internal comparisons rather than rigorous AI-vs-traditional operational benchmarks, and a few claims lean on inference rather than explicit comparative evidence. Overall, the answer meets the criterion with strong core examples, though tighter citation discipline would improve robustness.

Below is a mechanistic and algorithmic synthesis of how AI systems optimize lubricant viscosity to increase load-carrying capacity in boundary lubrication (BL), drawing on tribology theory, Stribeck mapping, and machine‑learning frameworks for lubricant design and testing.

1) Why viscosity matters for load capacity in boundary/mixed lubrication
- In BL and mixed regimes, total load is split between asperity contact and thin fluid films; increasing viscosity thickens the separating film and shifts load away from direct asperity contact, thereby raising load-carrying capacity and lowering friction when operation lands in a better regime on the Stribeck curve <cite id="d82ae4d1-0">In the mixed lubrication condition, both direct contact of surface asperities and dynamic pressure of the oil film are present, and the load carried by the hydrodynamic pressure increases as the oil film grows in thickness; in hydrodynamic lubrication, the entire load is carried by hydrodynamic pressure</cite> <cite id="d82ae4d1-1">Wear of tribo-material happens under boundary and mixed lubrication regimes where direct surface-surface contact occurs</cite> <cite id="d82ae4d1-2">In general, we can use lower viscosity lubricants for fast-running machines and heavy-load machines need higher viscosity lubricants; lubricants should support all regimes from hydrodynamic to boundary</cite> <cite id="d82ae4d1-4">The boundary lubrication regime is characterized by a high COF with surface asperities supporting the load; in mixed lubrication both asperities and lubricant support the load; in hydrodynamic lubrication the load is supported by lubricant hydrodynamic pressure with low COF</cite>.
- The Stribeck framework quantifies this through the dimensionless Hersey/Sommerfeld numbers: higher viscosity (for fixed speed/load) moves operation toward regimes with thinner boundary films and lower asperity loading, reducing friction and wear until hydrodynamic regime is reached; conversely, low viscosity at high load/low speed forces BL/mixed operation with higher friction and contact stress <cite id="d82ae4d1-0">The Sommerfeld number links viscosity, velocity, and load to partition lubrication between boundary, mixed, and hydrodynamic regimes</cite> <cite id="d82ae4d1-4">The Stribeck curve plots friction coefficient versus a Hersey number built from dynamic viscosity, sliding velocity, and unit load</cite> <cite id="d82ae4d1-2">For fixed conditions, friction increases as viscosity increases under hydrodynamic lubrication, implying viscosity must be tuned to a proper level; additive technology is used to control viscosity</cite>.
- Practical guidance from Stribeck-based analyses: heavier loads and lower speeds call for higher viscosity to maintain a thicker separating film and avoid boundary contact; however, the Stribeck curve is an approximation and under BL/mixed regimes friction and wear are sensitive to surface roughness and chemistry, which complicates viscosity-only control <cite id="d82ae4d1-1">The Stribeck curve does not fully support boundary and mixed lubrication regimes but indicates inferior performance there compared to hydrodynamic lubrication</cite> <cite id="d82ae4d1-2">Lower viscosity is favored for hydrodynamic operation; heavy-load machines need higher viscosity lubricants; lubricants must support all regimes due to start-stop conditions</cite>.

2) AI/ML objectives and models for optimizing viscosity under BL
- AI systems cast the optimization as a multi-objective problem: maximize film thickness/load capacity at given speed/load/temperature while controlling friction, oxidation, and viscosity stability; neural networks and Bayesian models learn mappings from lubricant composition, viscosity grade, additives, and operating variables to friction, film thickness, and wear, enabling virtual screening and surrogate-guided design <cite id="eeb7fc05-2">Tribologists and computer scientists co-develop ML tools to predict optimum lubricants and parameters, reducing trial-and-error and improving performance and reliability</cite> <cite id="5917fab8-1">ML predicts viscosity, coefficient of friction, wear, and film thickness under diverse conditions, identifying correlations between chemistry, operating parameters, and performance to tailor lubricants and reduce experimentation</cite> <cite id="5917fab8-3">A deep learning model accurately predicts Stribeck curves across conditions, supporting formulation and system optimization with the caveat that predictions are optimal within the training data domain</cite>.
- Data-driven models explicitly capture viscosity’s role in film thickness and load capacity, allowing AI to optimize operating points (viscosity grade, temperature) and candidate lubricants (base oil + additives) to lift load capacity under BL. For example, a Bayesian-optimized BP network predicted film thickness and load-carrying capacity from viscosity and other inputs, showing a strong positive correlation between viscosity and lubrication performance and enabling automated hyperparameter tuning to find high-load/low-wear operating maps <cite id="eeb7fc05-1">A Bayesian-optimized neural network predicted film thickness and load-carrying capacity from viscosity, applied load, sliding speed, and contact inclination, showing a significant positive correlation between viscosity and lubrication performance and enabling efficient screening of HA-based lubricants</cite>.
- Mixed-lubrication-aware models help AI reason about regime transitions: multi-MLP ANNs separate hydrodynamic and solid/asperity contact contributions to pressure and wear, allowing optimization of viscosity and surface/operational parameters to move contact area into a higher-film-thickness regime and reduce load on asperities <cite id="eeb7fc05-0">An ANN modeled mixed lubrication by partitioning load between hydrodynamic and solid contacts; separate MLPs predicted hydrodynamic and solid contact pressures, friction, and wear, enabling optimization over viscosity and operating parameters to improve lubricated contact performance</cite>.

3) How AI optimizes lubricant viscosity and additives to raise load capacity
- Formulation optimization loop: AI-guided design searches base oil viscosity grades and additive packages (viscosity modifiers, VI improvers, friction modifiers) to meet viscosity targets at temperature while maximizing friction/wear outcomes, using Bayesian optimization to cut experiments. For example, models that predict film thickness and load-carrying capacity vs. friction show that there is an optimal viscosity/temperature window that maximizes safe load under BL before friction begins to rise in hydrodynamic regimes; AI selects that window via constrained optimization or Pareto front exploration <cite id="eeb7fc05-1">A Bayesian-optimized neural network predicted film thickness and load-carrying capacity and frictional behavior, showing how viscosity correlates with lubrication performance and enabling efficient optimization over operating parameters and lubricant candidates</cite> <cite id="5917fab8-1">AI uncovers correlations between lubricant chemistry and operating parameters to tailor solutions that improve efficiency and reduce costs, reflecting multi-objective trade-offs</cite>.

- Diagnose operating maps: Use AI models of Stribeck behavior to identify BL/mixed regimes and the viscosity–film-thickness–load-capacity relationships at current base oil/additive choices <cite id="d82ae4d1-0">Stribeck analysis links viscosity, speed, and load to regime and load sharing between film and asperities</cite> <cite id="eeb7fc05-1">Neural-network surrogates predict film thickness and load capacity from viscosity and operating variables</cite>.

Snippet: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) is fundamentally revolutionizing lubricant design, displacing traditional trial-and-error methods with data-driven precision. By leveraging vast datasets on material properties, chemical compositions, and performance metrics, ML algorithms can rapidly identify optimal formulations that minimize friction, reduce wear, and enhance durability, drastically accelerating the development cycle [128,129]. 

A key strength of ML lies in its ability to decode the complex, non-linear relationships between molecular structures and tribological performance. Techniques such as neural networks and genetic algorithms excel at uncovering hidden patterns in the interactions between base oils, additives, and operational environments. This enables the creation of lubricants tailored for highly specific applications. Furthermore, physics-informed ML integrates fundamental domain knowledge with data-driven insights, producing interpretable and scientifically grounded models that accurately predict performance under extreme temperatures and pressures [130]. 

AI and ML are also reshaping the validation process. ML-powered virtual simulations can replicate real-world operating conditions, predicting critical outcomes like oxidation stability and viscosity changes with high accuracy. This capability significantly reduces the reliance on costly and time-consuming physical tests, allowing engineers to refine and screen formulations computationally before they ever enter a laboratory [131]. 

While the potential is vast, challenges in data quality, availability, and model interpretability remain. The next frontier involves developing hybrid models that create a collaborative loop between experimental data, AI-driven predictions, and human expertise. By overcoming these hurdles, AI and ML are poised to unlock unprecedented efficiencies, paving the way for the rapid creation of smarter, greener, and more resilient lubricant solutions.
</snippet>

Snippet: Trial-and-error formulation strategies continue to dominate additive discovery and base oil blending. The identification of formulations that satisfy viscosity targets, oxidation stability, friction reduction, and wear protection often requires hundreds of iterative experiments, especially when additives interact in nonlinear ways across concentration and operating conditions. Bayesian optimization directly addresses this bottleneck by guiding experimental campaigns towards promising regions of formulation space using probabilistic surrogate models, reducing the number of physical tests required while maintaining performance targets [3][4][5][6]. 

Limited transferability of empirical structure-property correlations further constrains predictive formulation design. Classical relationships often break down when applied to new base oils, additive chemistries, or emerging sustainable candidates such as ionic liquids and deep eutectic solvents. Structure-property learning frameworks, including QSPR and QSTR, improve generalization by learning nonlinear mappings between molecular descriptors and macroscopic lubricant behavior, enabling prediction of viscosity, friction, and wear trends across diverse chemistries where traditional regression models are insufficient [13]. 

The dependence on long-duration endurance and field testing remains another major barrier for rapid screening. Engine and fleet trials are essential for final validation but are impractical for evaluating large candidate sets. ML predictors trained on laboratory measurements, molecular descriptors, or spectroscopic data help narrow candidate pools early by forecasting key properties such as viscosity evolution and oxidation stability, thereby concentrating experimental resources on the most promising formulations [4,5]. 

Finally, conventional diagnostics and maintenance practices remain largely reactive. Standard methods such as ferrography, viscometry, and spectroscopy provide valuable information but typically require offline sampling and expert interpretation, limiting scalability for continuous monitoring. AI enables a shift toward predictive maintenance by automating wear debris classification, integrating multimodal sensor streams, and embedding these insights within digital twin frameworks that forecast lubricant degradation and remaining useful life [7][8][9].

Snippet: Petroleum products rely on additives to enhance performance across transportation, construction, and energy sectors. These additives regulate viscosity, friction, wear resistance, and thermal stability. Traditional additive research depends on empirical trial and error, which is slow, costly, and limited in scope. Recently, machine learning (ML) methods have been applied to identify complex structure–property relationships, predict performance before experimentation, and guide formulation strategies. This review presents a unified framework for ML integration into petroleum additive research, organizing existing studies into a systematic taxonomy that links data modalities, algorithmic choices, and application domains. It overviews taxonomy of ML tasks and a unified framework that maps data types, methods, and application domains relevant to lubrication science. Through representative examples, the review illustrates the breadth of current applications, ranging from gallate additive design using deep neural networks informed by quantum‐scale data, to asphalt binder optimization through predictive modeling, and the screening of lubricants using statistical and tree‐based methods, and highlights emerging efforts that apply deep learning to real‐time lubricant degradation and condition monitoring through multi‐sensor data fusion. The review provides a practical roadmap for addressing the key limitations and accelerating additive discovery, enhancing predictive maintenance, and supporting the development of more sustainable lubricant formulations.

The Stribeck curve shows the friction coefficient and oil film thickness at the hydraulic bearing based on the Sommerfeld number, which is calculated by multiplying the fluid viscosity by the relative velocity and dividing it by the load. Depending on the Sommerfeld number, the lubrication conditions are divided into boundary lubrication, mixed lubrication, and hydrodynamic lubrication conditions [27]. The boundary lubrication condition occurs when the relative velocity and fluid viscosity are low or the load is high, during which the asperities on both surfaces are in direct contact or the two surfaces are separated by an oil film that is monolayered or multilayered. In the mixed lubrication condition, both direct contact of surface asperities and dynamic pressure of the oil film are present, and the load carried by the hydrodynamic pressure increases as the oil film grows in thickness. In the hydrodynamic lubrication condition, both surfaces are completely separated by the fluid, and the entire load is carried by the hydrodynamic pressure [28].

This approximation is realistic if the molecular boundary layer is assumed to be incompressible. The modelling of a mixed lubrication regime where the hydrodynamic pressure and the solid contact pressure allows to investigate the main characteristics of the lubricated contact have been investigated numerically for various cases [8,9].
